Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The rhythm New things on the way Wardens The Toll Why it matters Deep in a run: the top bar names the hour and when it strikes. When the mainspring runs down, ring back or recast. The clock face on the bell tower tracks your run. The top of the screen shows where you are, with something like "3 o'clock, strikes at wave 41". The rhythm A wave arrives about every 30 seconds, or sooner if you call it early. Every 10 waves the hand moves one hour. The day starts at 12 o'clock. When an hour strikes, a Warden arrives, a mini-boss that is a large one of the newest kind of wind-up on the ground. At midnight, wave 120, the Toll comes , a boss. Then the day starts again, and the next Toll comes at wave 240, then 360 and so on. Wave What comes 10, 20, 30, ... A Warden 120 The Toymaker's Drummer 240 The Miller's Grindstone 360 The Postmaster 480 The Founder's Golem 600 onward The four Tolls come round again in the same order Waves 120, 240 and so on bring a Toll instead of a Warden. New things on the way The first time each kind of wind-up appears, the wave preview marks it "new". Tickers begin at wave 1, Scuttlers at 10, Platebacks at 20, Gliders at 31, and one new kind each hour after that until the Conductors at wave 81. See The wind-ups . Wardens Each Warden drops a lot of Parts, and there is a chance, far higher than for ordinary wind-ups, that it wakes and joins you as crew. Wardens count towards the Bell-metal you earn when you recast. More on Wardens and Tolls . The Toll A Toll is a huge bell-ringer from one of the valley's old workshops. Stopping one pays a lot of Bell-metal and moves the story on. Each Toll has its own tricks; see Wardens and Tolls (spoilers) and The story . Why it matters Planning: a Warden is due every tenth wave, so spend your Parts before it arrives. Twists: some valleys and twists change reach, speed or Parts for the whole run. Short Day: one of the Trials brings midnight forward to wave 60. Tip Check the top bar before a big wave. If the hand is about to strike, a Warden is the last wind-up of the wave. s: The seeded Daily Valley, the fortnightly Peal competition and the Google Play Games boards.
x: Home The Last Bell Systems Daily Valley, the Peal and leaderboards Daily Valley, the Peal and leaderboards The seeded Daily Valley, the fortnightly Peal competition and the Google Play Games boards. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The Daily Valley The Peal Leaderboards Monthly valley Tips A hand-made valley. The Daily Valley and the Peal draw from the everyday valley, the first five hand-made valleys and, for the Peal, the Open Field. There are a few fixed challenges you can measure yourself against. All are optional, and none of them touches your main valley's progress. The Daily Valley A small, seeded run that is the same for everyone on the same day (UTC). It opens after your first recast. Its own world: every attempt starts from scratch, with no Foundry or stars. The valley and its twists: each day draws a valley and two twists. See Twists . The roads are the same for everyone that day. The reward: reach the day's target wave once and you receive a little Bell-metal in your main valley. The target is set from your best wave (about a fifth of it, but never less than wave 8 and never more than wave 35). Attempts: as many as you like; the best wave of the day is kept. There is no chat and no leaderboard for the Daily Valley. The Peal The Peal is a fortnightly competition, named after a long performance of bell changes. A new Peal begins every 14 days (on a Monday, 00:00 UTC). You opt in. It never interrupts the main game. A separate world from scratch. Joining gives you a fresh keeper for that Peal only, with no Bell-metal, no Foundry and towers starting from the beginning. What you earn in the Peal stays in the Peal. The same conditions for everyone: one valley and two modifiers, so the roads are the same for all. Score: the best wave reached in that Peal's world. Groups of 100. You are placed in a group; when one fills, a new one opens. Your group's board shows names and best waves only. There is no chat, no messages, no interaction. At the end, everyone who played receives some Bell-metal in the main valley, with more for a higher place: 400 for first, 250 for the top three, 150 for the top ten (or tenth of the group), 80 for the top half, and 40 for taking part. Fair play: a wave cannot be reached faster than its waves can honestly arrive. The Peal uses your Play Games name and its scores are shown to your group. Leaderboards If you sign in to Google Play Games from Settings, three boards track your best wave, the Wardens you have mended and the Tolls you have stopped. Signing in is optional and play never depends on it. Monthly valley Each calendar month a valley is featured, with a twist. See Valleys and Twists and the monthly valley . Tips Everyone starts from scratch in both, so tower pairings and good pad choices matter more than stars. Read the twists before you start. "Short Memory" removes Hindsight and "Lean Valley" gives you only six pads. They are also a safe place to try a new idea without risking a good run. Previous Trials Next Crew and the Roll

s: How mended wind-ups sometimes wake and join your defence, and how the Roll remembers them.
x: Home The Last Bell Systems Crew and the Roll Crew and the Roll How mended wind-ups sometimes wake and join your defence, and how the Roll remembers them. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Waking Crew The Roll Tips Any of these can wake as crew. The great Tolls at the bottom never do. Most mended wind-ups lie down and stay down. Occasionally one wakes up and joins you as crew. Tamsin wrote that some of them always would: "Wind them with kindness and a few will wind back." Waking Every mend has a small chance of waking the wind-up: about one in 400 for the plainest kinds, a little better for tougher ones, and about fifteen times as likely for a Warden . A Toll never wakes. Waking has its own luck, so it never changes the roads or the waves. Crew A woken wind-up becomes crew . You place it in a tower (one crew member per tower), and it adds its own strength: Wind-up What its crew adds Ticker +15 percent strikes Scuttler +25 percent speed Plateback +25 percent strikes Glider +20 percent reach Spinner +20 percent speed, +10 percent strikes Cluster +20 percent strikes Oiler +15 percent speed, +15 percent strikes Brollyback +30 percent strikes Conductor +35 percent speed Any Warden extra +25 percent strikes and +20 percent speed on top Crew serve for the run that woke them. The Roll The first time a kind wakes, it is written on the Roll for good. The Roll is kept through every recast, and each later waking of the same kind makes that crew stronger: its bonus grows by a tenth for every waking after the first, up to double. The Foundry's Crew quarters upgrade lets you start each run with crew from the Roll, the strongest first (Wardens first, then the latest kinds), up to three. Tips Put speed-crew (Scuttler, Conductor) in fast towers and strike-crew (Brollyback, Plateback) in heavy hitters. A Warden's crew is the best, so every Warden you stop is a small chance at a strong helper. The Roll lists every kind of wind-up that has woken so far, if you want to check what you're missing. s: The small glowing moth of the belfry, who settles by one tower at a time and remembers when the bell rings back.
x: Home The Last Bell Systems The lantern moth The lantern moth The small glowing moth of the belfry, who settles by one tower at a time and remembers when the bell rings back. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The moth remembers In the opening In the world The lantern moth of the belfry. The moth lives in the belfry. During a run it drifts about the field on its own and settles near one tower at a time. While it rests there, that tower strikes 20 percent harder . Every minute or two it moves on to another tower. It prefers Light towers. A Light-family tower (Lantern post, Orrery, Starwheel) is three times as likely to be chosen as any other, so if you build one you will see the moth more often. The moth remembers When you ring the bell back, almost everything returns to how it was half a minute ago, including wind-ups, Parts, towers and the mainspring. The moth doesn't. It stays where it was. It can't be harmed and it has no attack. Nothing happens to it while you are away. In the opening The moth talks you through your first run, giving each step as you finish the last. Tip If the moth is sitting beside a tower that matters (your best striker), leave that tower alone for now. Moving or selling a tower it has settled by sends it elsewhere. In the world A lantern moth appears in every BlairsLab game. Here it lives in the belfry. See also The story and Rewind the minute . Previous Crew and the Roll Next Towers at a glance

s: How towers, rarities, families, limits, levels, stars and final forms fit together in The Last Bell.
x: Home The Last Bell Towers Towers at a glance Towers at a glance How towers, rarities, families, limits, levels, stars and final forms fit together in The Last Bell. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Rarities Field limits How towers unlock Levels inside a run Stars, forever Final forms Families Reach The bell tower you defend. Everything you build is there to keep it ringing. Towers are built with Parts during a run, and each one has a rarity, a family and its own way of working. This page covers the rules that apply to all of them. The pages for each rarity list every tower. Rarities Rarity Frame colour Where to read about it Common stone grey Common towers Uncommon verdigris Uncommon towers Rare blue Rare towers Epic violet Epic towers (spoilers) Legendary gold Legendary, Mythic and Exalted (spoilers) Mythic crimson same page Exalted pale white-gold same page Higher rarities are stronger and cost more Parts, but fewer of them may stand on the field at once. Every tower also has its own shape, so you don't have to rely on colour to tell rarity. Field limits Rarity At most on the field Common and Uncommon as many as you have pads Rare 4 Epic 2 Legendary 1 Mythic 1 Exalted 1 How towers unlock Towers unlock by the best wave you have ever reached , in any run. You begin with the Clapper, Spring-gun and Chime post. Each other tower has its own wave. A few Trials unlock a tower early; see Trials . Levels inside a run Within a run a tower can be raised to level 10 . Each level makes the tower strike harder (damage grows by about 45 percent a level) and reach a little further (about 3 percent), but each upgrade costs about 62 percent more than the last. Selling returns 70 percent. Stars, forever Separately, each tower has a permanent star rating, bought with Bell-metal in the Foundry . Each star makes that tower strike 25 percent harder in every later run, compounding, up to 15 stars. The first star costs 25 Bell-metal for a Common tower, and more for higher rarities (40, 65, 100, 150, 225 and 300 for Uncommon through Exalted). Each further star costs about 45 percent more than the last. Final forms At level 10, each tower chooses one of two final forms , each with its own painting. For example, the Spring-gun becomes a Repeater (fires twice as fast) or a Harpoon (each bolt pierces up to three wind-ups in a line). The choice lasts for that tower in that run, so you can choose differently next time. Every form is listed on the rarity pages. Families Every tower belongs to one of seven families: Bell, Spring, Weight, Air, Light, Oil and Time. Families matter for a few things. Fliers: Spring, Bell and Air towers can generally strike fliers (Gliders); Weight and Oil towers cannot. Each tower's card says so, and so do the pages here. Pairings: some towers reward being used together. See Tower pairings . The moth prefers to settle near Light towers. See The lantern moth . Reach Reach is measured in tiles of the field, which is 11 tiles across. Fog and some Trials shorten reach for every tower. Lantern posts and similar towers lengthen it for their neighbours. Tip One kind of tower won't cover everything. Armour, fliers, healers and umbrellas each need a different counter, and The wind-ups lists them. Previous The lantern moth Next Common towers

Commons make up most of every run. You can build as many as you have pads, and permanent stars make them strike harder in every later run. Tower Family Cost (Parts) Damage Strikes per second Reach (tiles) Opens at best wave Clapper Bell 20 6 1.0 2.2 start Spring-gun Spring 35 2.2 3.5 2.6 start Chime post Bell 50 4 0.8 2.0 start Weight-drop Weight 45 22 0.35 1.8 8 Tack-thrower Spring 40 4 0.4 2.0 14 Bellows Air 55 1 0.4 1.6 20 The figures are for a level 1 tower, before upgrades and stars. Clapper Steady single strikes. A Bell-family tower that hits fliers as well as ground wind-ups, and the usual first tower. Great Clapper: heavier strikes that stun the wind-up for a moment. Twin Peal: strikes two wind-ups at once. Spring-gun Fast, light shots. The best tower for finishing weak, fast wind-ups like Scuttlers, and it can hit fliers. Repeater: fires twice as fast. Harpoon: each bolt pierces up to three wind-ups in a line. Very good on a long straight road. Chime post A small splash around its target. Good against clumps and against Clusters, and it hits fliers. Wind Chimes: a much wider splash. Resonator: wind-ups it strikes ring for 3 seconds, and every tower hits them 25 percent harder. Weight-drop Slow, crushing blows that shrug off armour. This is your answer to Platebacks. It cannot reach fliers. Anvil: more than twice the damage, a little slower. Tremor: shakes the ground, with a splash that stops wind-ups for a moment. Weight towers hit a wind-up harder if a Magnet coil has pulled its plates off. See Tower pairings . Tack-thrower Scatters tacks on the road; wind-ups walking over them are hurt. It works on the ground only, so it cannot reach fliers. Caltrops: tacks last twice as long and slow whatever walks on them. Brass Shrapnel: twice the damage over a wider spread. Bellows Puffs everything nearby back down the road. It nudges wind-ups backwards so your other towers have more time on them. Gale: pushes twice as far. Organ Pipe: blasts fliers, with four times the damage and a longer push against Gliders. Which commons to start with? A Clapper or Spring-gun on each road is a fine start. Add a Chime post where wind-ups bunch, then a Weight-drop once it opens at wave 8, so you have one ready when Platebacks arrive at wave 20. Next: Uncommon towers . Tip The Tack-thrower and Bellows do little alone, but they make every other tower near them more useful because wind-ups spend longer in reach. Previous Towers at a glance Next Uncommon towers

Each rare tower answers a particular kind of wind-up or the long haul of a deep run. No more than four can stand on the field at once, so choose them carefully. They open between waves 70 and 110. Tower Family Cost Damage Strikes per second Reach Opens at best wave Escapement Time 140 20 1.2 2.4 70 Magnet coil Weight 150 14 0.8 2.3 75 Bell mortar Bell 170 48 0.3 3.6 80 Sounding horn Air 130 none 0.25 2.2 90 Spring trap Spring 135 12 0.25 1.6 95 Scrap cart Oil 120 none n/a 1.8 100 Mender's post Time 160 none 0.2 1.0 110 Escapement Every third strike stops its wind-up dead for a moment. It cannot reach fliers. Anchor: every second strike stops its wind-up. Verge: its stopping strike catches everything near the wind-up too. Magnet coil Pulls the plates off what it strikes , so it has no casing for a while and Weight towers hit it harder. It cannot reach fliers. It pairs well with the Weight-drop against Platebacks. Lodestone: plates stay off twice as long. Arc Coil: each strike arcs to three wind-ups nearby and strips them too. Bell mortar Lobs heavy bell-shells a long way into the thickest crowd. Its reach of 3.6 tiles is the longest of the early towers. Siege Bell: twice the damage and a wider blast, a little slower. Carpet Peal: three shells at once, each a little lighter. Sounding horn Marks everything in reach, fliers too. Marked wind-ups take more from every tower, and its blast folds a Brollyback's umbrella. It does no damage itself, but it makes every other tower stronger. Foghorn: carries half as far again, and its marks last twice as long. Hunting Horn: marked wind-ups also walk a quarter slower, fliers too. Spring trap Sets a spring on the road beside it. The first wind-up to step on it is flung back down the road , then the spring winds itself again. It cannot catch fliers. Double Spring: winds itself again twice as fast. Bear Trap: holds what it catches for two seconds, and bites twice as hard. Scrap cart Wind-ups mended near it give 50 percent more Parts. It strikes nothing. Salvage Wagon: wind-ups mended near it give twice the Parts. Tinker's Cart: gathers from twice as far away. Mender's post Winds the bell tower's mainspring back up a little every few seconds. In a long run it helps you outlast leaks. Great Spring: winds the mainspring twice as much. Watchman: each winding also helps the bell gather its next rewind. Picking rares With only four slots, pick for what your run needs. A Sounding horn helps when Brollybacks and fliers show up, a Mender's post when leaks are steady, a Scrap cart early in a run to build faster, and an Escapement or Spring trap to buy seconds. A Magnet coil beside a Weight-drop works well, since the plates come off and the Weight-drop hits harder. See Tower pairings . Next: Epic towers (spoilers). Previous Uncommon towers Next Epic towers

s: Every kind of clockwork wind-up in The Last Bell, when it first appears, how it behaves and what beats it.
x: Home The Last Bell Enemies The wind-ups The wind-ups Every kind of clockwork wind-up in The Last Bell, when it first appears, how it behaves and what beats it. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The roster Ticker Scuttler Plateback Glider Spinner Cluster Oiler Brollyback Conductor Mixed waves The wind-ups, in order of arrival, and the four great Tolls at the bottom (spoilers for later pages). Wind-ups are old toys and tools that ran down and rusted. Your towers mend them rather than destroy them. Each kind has its own silhouette, one visible trait and one obvious counter, so you can read a wave from the strip under the field. The roster Wind-up First appears Base health Speed Harm to the bell Parts when mended Ticker wave 1 10 0.9 4 3 Scuttler wave 10 6 1.7 3 3 Plateback wave 20 30 0.6 8 8 Glider wave 31 9 1.1 5 5 Spinner wave 41 12 0.8 5 5 Cluster wave 51 14 0.8 6 3 Oiler wave 61 16 0.75 4 6 Brollyback wave 71 20 0.7 7 7 Conductor wave 81 18 0.85 5 7 These are the values at wave 1. Health, Parts and harm all grow with each wave: health by about 11.5 percent a wave up to wave 50, then by 7 percent a wave. Ticker The basic walker, round and rusty. You will mend thousands of them. Scuttler Fast and fragile. A mechanical beetle. Quick towers like the Spring-gun are ideal, and a Bellows or a Damper buys time. Plateback Slow and armoured. A clockwork tortoise. Its casing takes a little off every strike, which punishes fast, weak shots. Answer with the Weight-drop , which shrugs off armour, or pull the plates off with a Magnet coil . Glider Fliers on paper wings. Gliders ignore the roads and fly straight at the bell , so some of your towers must stand near it. Only Spring, Bell and Air towers can strike them (check each tower's card). They cannot be slowed by oil or a Damper, and a Catchwheel cannot drag them. The Weathercock is the specialist. Spinner A spinning-top with a crossbow. It stops at range and throws bolts at your towers . A bolt jams the nearest tower for 1.5 seconds, every 4 seconds. Kill it quickly, or keep strong towers out of its range. Cluster Three Tickers clumped together. Stop it and it comes apart into all three. Splash towers like the Chime post make quick work of the pieces. Oiler A walking oil can that oils the wind-ups around it back to health (about 4 percent of their health every second). Pick it off first. Brollyback A soldier with an umbrella. The umbrella soaks up half its health in strikes and opens again if it is left alone for 4 seconds. Steady fire keeps it folded, and the Sounding horn 's blast folds it immediately. Conductor A conductor with a baton who winds up the wind-ups around him so they walk 30 percent faster. Kill him first. Mixed waves From wave 31 onwards, waves mix kinds, and more join every ten waves. The 41st wave, for instance, adds Spinners to a wave already holding Tickers, Scuttlers, Platebacks and Gliders. The wave preview under the field tells you what is coming and marks each new kind. Every hour on the clock a Warden comes, a large one of the newest kind of wind-up, and at midnight the Toll comes. See The clock face for the schedule and Tower pairings for answers. Tip The mended sometimes wake and join you. See Crew and the Roll . Previous Tower pairings Next Wardens and Tolls

s: The mini-bosses that strike each hour and the four great Tolls at midnight, with their tricks and how to stop them.
x: Home The Last Bell Enemies Wardens and Tolls Wardens and Tolls The mini-bosses that strike each hour and the four great Tolls at midnight, with their tricks and how to stop them. Updated 11 November 2026 Spoilers ahead. This page discusses story events and reveals. Come back after you have played if you want to find things out yourself. On this page Wardens The Tolls The Toymaker's Drummer (wave 120) The Miller's Grindstone (wave 240) The Postmaster (wave 360) The Founder's Golem (wave 480) Tips Warning This page names the Tolls and their stories. Skip it if you would like to meet them cold. The opening of the story: every clock in the valley stopped on the same evening. Only one bell kept ringing. Wardens Tamsin's notebook says the Wardens were the valley's finest work: one stood at every workshop gate and struck the hour as it passed. When the Rust came, they walked with the rest. In the game a Warden arrives as the last wind-up of every tenth wave, as the hour strikes. It is a large version of the newest kind of wind-up on the ground: at wave 10 a Scuttler, at 20 a Plateback, and so on up to a Conductor from wave 90. It is bigger, slower, heavier on the bell and far tougher than the others, and it pays much more. A Warden is also far more likely to wake and join you: roughly fifteen times as likely as an ordinary wind-up of its kind. See Crew and the Roll . The Tolls A Toll comes at midnight every 120 waves. Four Tolls come in turn and then the cycle repeats. A Toll can never wake as crew. Each pays a very large amount of Parts and, when you recast, a big share of Bell-metal. The Toymaker's Drummer (wave 120) Led the valley's parade every midsummer, from the toymaker's door to the bell. Its drumbeat makes every wind-up on the field walk faster (by a quarter) for as long as it stands, so stop it early. It is slow and armoured. The Miller's Grindstone (wave 240) The mill's great stone rolled out of the door and down the road. It rolls in bursts , running much faster for a moment, and sheds a ring of four Platebacks at half strength. Bring something that handles armour, such as the Weight-drop or Magnet coil. The Postmaster (wave 360) Never stopped trying to deliver the valley's letters. It posts flocks of Gliders as it walks , and a great many at half strength. Have fliers covered: a Weathercock and Bell towers near the bell. The Founder's Golem (wave 480) Tamsin's own helper, cast in her moulds. At half strength it recasts itself : for about 3 seconds it is molten and untouchable, and then whole again. Don't waste your big strikes while it is molten. Once the Golem is mended, you reach Tamsin's foundry. Tips All Tolls are slow, well under half a Ticker's pace, so slows and holds count for more than raw damage. Against the Drummer and Golem, open with your heaviest hits. Against the Grindstone and Postmaster, cover what they spawn. The Short Day Trial brings the Drummer forward to wave 60. See also The clock face , Tips for deep waves and The story . Previous The wind-ups Next The valleys

s: Wandering Roads, nine hand-made valleys and the Open Field: how each is unlocked and what makes it different.
x: Home The Last Bell Maps The valleys The valleys Wandering Roads, nine hand-made valleys and the Open Field: how each is unlocked and what makes it different. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Wandering Roads Hand-made valleys The Open Field Picking a valley Water and trees Twists The Mill Race, one of the hand-made valleys. A valley is the ground you defend, with its roads, pads and scenery. There are three kinds. Wandering Roads The everyday valley. It begins every run with two roads , and they wind a new way every run, so you have to make a slightly different plan each time. Most players spend most of their time here. Hand-made valleys Nine hand-made valleys have fixed roads and their own ground and scenery. Each opens when your best wave reaches a set number: Valley Opens at best wave Layout The Crossroads 15 Four short roads from every side like a pinwheel Switchback Hill 25 One long road zig-zagging up the heath The Spiral 35 A single road coiling round the tower The Mill Race 45 A stream crossed by two plank bridges, plus a road from the west Orchard Rows 55 Two long straight rows between apple trees The Ring Road 65 One great road that laps the bell twice The Forked Brook 75 A brook splits in two, with a road along each bank The Narrows 85 Two long straight lanes between hedges Market Square 95 Four short lanes spilling into a crowded square The full guide is on Hand-made valleys . The Open Field No roads at all: you build the maze. It opens after your first recast. See The Open Field . Picking a valley After a few runs, the Foundry's start screen offers Wandering Roads, the featured monthly valley, any hand-made valleys you have unlocked, and Trials . Wandering Roads is always available. Water and trees Water and trees are tiles nothing can be built on. A road that crosses water is a bridge, as on the Mill Race and the Forked Brook. Twists Any valley can be played with a twist : the monthly valley, the Daily Valley and the Peal all add them. The featured monthly valley is always one of the first five hand-made valleys. Tip Hand-made valleys are the same every run, so they are a good way to learn where the best pads are. Previous Wardens and Tolls Next Hand-made valleys

s: A guide to each of the nine hand-made valleys of The Last Bell and how to play them.
x: Home The Last Bell Maps Hand-made valleys Hand-made valleys A guide to each of the nine hand-made valleys of The Last Bell and how to play them. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The Crossroads Switchback Hill The Spiral The Mill Race Orchard Rows The Ring Road The Forked Brook The Narrows Market Square Good habits on every map Orchard Rows at wave 7: two straight roads and the bell in the middle. Each hand-made valley has a fixed layout, so you can learn it. The unlock waves are on The valleys . The Crossroads Four short roads turn in from every side like the arms of a pinwheel. There are plenty of pads. Short roads mean little time to strike, so favour burst damage and holds, and keep towers close to the bell where several roads end. Switchback Hill One long road zig-zags up the heath to the bell. There are few places to build, so choose them carefully. A single long road suits slows and traps at its start and big strikers at the bends. The Spiral A single road coils round and round the tower before it arrives. Towers in the middle reach several turns at once. Put your reach and area towers in the centre. The Mill Race A mill stream runs through the valley; two roads cross it on plank bridges, a third comes in from the west. The roads meet at the bridges, so towers beside them cover more than one road. Nothing can be built on the water. Orchard Rows Two long straight rows between the apple trees. They are easy to cover, but the wind-ups come in long lines. A Cog-saw, Harpoon-form Spring-gun or Pendulum cuts down lines. Orchard trees also block building. The Ring Road One great road laps the bell twice, once round the outside and once round the inside, before it turns in. The pads between the laps reach both, so they are the prime spots. The Forked Brook A brook runs up to the bell and splits in two, with a road along each bank and a plank bridge over each branch. Hold one bank, or stretch to hold both. Decide early, because splitting your towers thins both defences. The Narrows Two long straight lanes run between hedges to the bell. Only the few pads in the middle can see down both of them, so put your best towers there and everything else at the ends of the lanes. Market Square Four short lanes spill into a crowded square. There is hardly any road to defend, so the wind-ups are on you almost at once. It gives you the least time of the early layouts, so spend your Parts fast and keep a rewind charge ready. Good habits on every map Look for pads that cover two stretches of road at once (inside corners, middles of spirals). Put slowers at the start of a road and strikers after it. Keep a few towers near the bell for fliers, since Gliders ignore roads. See The wind-ups . Use Tower pairings to turn a good pad into a great one. For maps with no roads at all, see The Open Field . Previous The valleys Next The Open Field

s: The maze mode: no roads, cheap stone walls, and a gate that wind-ups must find their way through.
x: Home The Last Bell Maps The Open Field The Open Field The maze mode: no roads, cheap stone walls, and a gate that wind-ups must find their way through. Updated 11 November 2026 A winding route past many towers. In the Open Field you shape the route yourself. The Open Field has no roads. Wind-ups come in at the gate and take the shortest way to the bell. You can build anywhere, and cheap stone walls let you make them walk the long way round. There must always be a way through, so you cannot wall the bell off completely. Rules It opens after your first recast. The field is bigger than the ordinary one (15 by 15 tiles instead of 11 by 11), to leave room for a maze. Stone walls cost 6 Parts and strike nothing. They exist only here, for steering. The whole map can be built on. It is its own world with its own Foundry, separate from your main valley's. How to play it Lengthen the route. The longer wind-ups walk in reach of your towers, the more strikes they take. Walls that make them double back are often worth more than another tower. Make corners. Put your strikers on the inside of turns, where a tower reaches several stretches of path at once. Keep the path open. Check there is still a way through as you build. Gliders ignore walls. They fly straight at the bell, so keep towers that hit fliers beside it. Slows and holds work well here, since the walls have already lengthened the walk. See The valleys and Tower pairings . Previous Hand-made valleys Next Twists and the monthly valley

s: Every twist that can change a valley, and how the monthly valley rotates.
x: Home The Last Bell Maps Twists and the monthly valley Twists and the monthly valley Every twist that can change a valley, and how the monthly valley rotates. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Every twist The monthly valley How to approach each twist The Mill Race: one of the five original hand-made valleys that the monthly valley draws from. A twist is a rule that changes a whole run. Some make it harder, some easier, and some do both. The monthly valley, the Daily Valley and the Peal all use twists. Every twist Twist What it does Fog Towers see 20 percent less far, but every mend gives twice the Parts Harvest Gliders arrive from wave 12 instead of 31 Brass Start with three times the Parts; wind-ups are 15 percent tougher Rust The mainspring holds 25 percent less, but the run is worth 50 percent more Bell-metal Iron Hour Every wind-up wears armour plates Swift Roads Wind-ups walk 15 percent faster, but give 25 percent more Parts Lean Valley Only six pads to build on, whatever the Foundry says Cheap Timber Towers cost 30 percent less to build and 30 percent more to upgrade Short Memory Ringing back the minute gives no Hindsight The monthly valley Each calendar month, one hand-made valley is featured with one of four twists (Fog, Harvest, Brass or Rust), the same for every player. Past months stay playable. The featured valley is chosen among the first five hand-made valleys, so it is always one you will already have unlocked: Crossroads, Switchback Hill, the Spiral, the Mill Race and Orchard Rows. See Hand-made valleys . How to approach each twist Fog. Place towers right beside the road. Splash and slows matter more, and Parts come quickly, so build wide. Harvest. Gliders turn up from wave 12. Build a Spring-gun, Gong or Bell tower near the bell by wave 10. Brass. You start with a big purse, so spend it on a strong set-up quickly, then keep upgrading. Rust. The mainspring is smaller. Rewind charges and a Mender's post help, and the payoff is extra Bell-metal. Iron Hour. Armour means Weight-drops and Magnet coils. Swift Roads. Slow them with a Damper, Oilcan or Kennel. Lean Valley. Choose your six pads carefully. Cheap Timber. Build lots and upgrade little. Short Memory. Each charge is a single use, as there is no stacking bonus. See Valleys , Daily Valley and the Peal and Trials . Previous The Open Field Next Tips for deep waves

s: Habits and layouts that carry a keeper from the first Warden to the late Tolls and beyond.
x: Home The Last Bell Reference Tips for deep waves Tips for deep waves Habits and layouts that carry a keeper from the first Warden to the late Tolls and beyond. Updated 11 November 2026 Spoilers ahead. This page discusses story events and reveals. Come back after you have played if you want to find things out yourself. On this page Before the run During the run Rewind habits Late towers The Tolls When you stall Warning Late-game advice that mentions towers and Tolls you may not have met yet. Wave 40: a mix of towers, with Tickers, Scuttlers, Platebacks and Gliders all in the next wave. Wind-up health grows by about 11.5 percent per wave up to wave 50, then 7 percent per wave. That is steep, so your towers have to keep pace. These habits help you keep up for longer. Before the run Spend Bell-metal in the right order. Truer strikes and Scavenging compound. The bell remembers and The bell keeps watch make runs safer. Put stars on the towers you actually use. Each star is 25 percent more strike, permanently. Keep research going. Use long projects overnight and short ones while you play. Choose your valley with care. A valley with a pad that covers two stretches of road beats one without it. During the run Build wide, then tall. Several towers early beat one upgraded one, up to the point where you have a pad on every stretch of road. Slows first, strikers after. Put a Damper, Oilcan, Kennel or Catchwheel at the start of a road and strikers beyond it. Keep fliers covered. From wave 31 Gliders ignore roads. Keep a Spring-gun, Bell tower or Gong near the bell. A Weathercock is the specialist. Armour needs weight. From wave 20 on, Platebacks shrug off weak shots. Use Weight-drops and Magnet coils. Kill the leaders. Spinners (from 41) jam towers, Oilers (61) heal everything near them and Conductors (81) speed everyone up. Splash towers hit the crowd, but a single strong striker removes the key wind-up. Break umbrellas. Brollybacks (71) shrug off hits until their umbrella folds. A Sounding horn or steady fire does it. Upgrade the best pads. The towers that see the most road are the ones to level. Call early when you are comfortable, and stop when a wave is stressing you. The bonus Parts aren't worth it if you start leaking. Watch the hour. A Warden arrives every tenth wave and a Toll at wave 120, 240, 360 and 480. Spend your Parts before they come. Rewind habits Learn from the echoes. Move something before you replay. Chain two rewinds to stack Hindsight, up to +30 percent. Don't spend your last charge on a leak you can recover from. Save it for a Warden or a Toll. Use The bell keeps watch if you leave runs playing. Late towers The Carillon (wave 361) chains its strikes and boosts every tower in reach. Put it in the middle of your cluster. Time towers (Still Point, Grand Escapement, Echo Spire, Second Hand) work well with each other and with your strikers. Pair stops with burst damage. The Starwheel and Long Pendulum cover the whole field, so they can go on any pad. Save the best pads for your specialists. See Legendary, Mythic and Exalted towers . The Tolls The Drummer speeds everyone up, so stop it first. The Grindstone sheds Platebacks, so have weight ready. The Postmaster posts Gliders, so cover fliers. The Golem goes molten at half health. Hold your biggest hits for when it isn't. When you stall If your runs stop improving, recast and spend. A fresh run with stronger stars and Foundry upgrades gets back to your old wave quickly and passes it.

s: Tamsin Hale's notebook, the valley's workshops and the pages that unlock as you stop each Toll.
x: Home The Last Bell Reference The story The story Tamsin Hale's notebook, the valley's workshops and the pages that unlock as you stop each Toll. Updated 11 November 2026 Spoilers ahead. This page discusses story events and reveals. Come back after you have played if you want to find things out yourself. On this page The opening The pages The valley The far hills No ending Warning Spoilers for the pages of story unlocked as you play, including all four Tolls. Every clock in the valley stopped on the same evening. Only one bell kept ringing. The opening Every clock in the valley stopped on the same evening. The mills fell still, the workshops went quiet. Only one bell kept ringing. It hangs in a small stone tower, kept for years by Tamsin Hale , bell-founder. She is gone now. She left you her notebook, and the key to the belfry. Out in the dark, the valley's old wind-ups are waking with Rust in their springs. They are not wicked, only broken, and the last ticking clock is calling them. Raise towers by the roads. Mend every wind-up you stop. And if a minute goes wrong, ring the bell backwards: Tamsin's notebook says you can. Wind-ups are stopped and mended, never killed. The pages The story comes in short pages that open at milestones. They stay in the Foundry's notebook so you can read them again. Page Opens when What it says The hour's guard you mend your first Warden The Wardens were the valley's finest work, one at every workshop gate, striking the hour as it passed Ringing backwards you ring back for the first time "Ring it the wrong way and it remembers the last minute, and lets you have it again. I only know it does, and that it tires." One who stayed a wind-up first wakes Some of them always would stay: "Wind them with kindness and a few will wind back" Recast your first recast Tamsin never threw a bell away; she melted it down and poured it again a little truer each time The toymaker's drummer the first Toll The Drummer led the valley's parade every midsummer. "Bring him home." The millstone the second Toll The mill fed the whole valley; its great stone rolled out of the door and the millrace has been still ever since Undelivered the third Toll Among the letters the Postmaster carried, one in Tamsin's own hand: "Thank you. Keep going." Tamsin's foundry the fourth Toll With the Golem mended you reach her foundry at last, her designs for the great bells pinned to its walls The valley The workshops that made the wind-ups were a toymaker's, a mill, a post office and a foundry. Each Toll comes from one of them. The legendary towers are Tamsin's own designs, found in her notebook as the story goes on. The far hills From the foundry's high window you can see, far across the hills, a tall tower with a lamp lit at the top, and beyond it a city standing still in the rain. The keeper doesn't know either place. No ending The story has no last page. Midnight just comes round again. See also The clock face and Wardens and Tolls . s: Quick answers about rewinding, recasting, unlocks, time away, Trials and more in The Last Bell.
x: Home The Last Bell Reference Frequently asked questions Frequently asked questions Quick answers about rewinding, recasting, unlocks, time away, Trials and more in The Last Bell. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Basics Rewind Progress Towers Away from the game Challenges The world The lantern moth. Basics What is The Last Bell? A hand-painted tower-defence game. You build towers beside the roads to stop clockwork wind-ups reaching the last bell tower, and you can ring the bell backwards to replay the last minute. See How to play . Do I need to sign in to anything? No. Signing in to Google Play Games is optional and play never depends on it. The Peal compares scores with a group of other keepers. Which languages does it have? Twelve. Is my run saved? Yes: your run is saved exactly where you left it. Rewind How many times can I rewind? You start with one charge. A charge comes back after 40 mends. The Foundry can raise the most the bell can hold to three, and speed up the recharge. See Rewind . How far back does it go? Thirty seconds. Does the same thing happen when I replay? Yes: the wind-ups come in the same order, the same way. What you changed is what makes the difference. What is Hindsight? Your towers strike 10 percent harder each time you replay a stretch (up to 30 percent). Progress What is Bell-metal? What a run melts into when you recast. It buys Foundry upgrades, tower stars and research. See Recast, Foundry and stars . What do I lose when I recast? Parts, the towers on the field, the wave count and the run's crew. You keep Bell-metal, unlocks, stars, the Foundry, research and the Roll. How do I unlock towers? By your best wave, in any run. Some Trials open an epic early. See Towers . How do I unlock valleys? Hand-made valleys open at best waves 15, 25, 35, and so on up to 95. See The valleys . When can I recast? When the run ends, or by choice from wave 20. Where did my Parts go? Parts only live during a run. Spend them as you go. Towers Why can't some towers hit Gliders? Weight and Oil towers cannot strike fliers; Spring, Bell and Air towers generally can. Each tower's card says so. What are final forms? At level 10 each tower chooses one of two final forms. Both are listed on the tower pages. Why can't I build another rare tower? Only four Rare, two Epic, and one each of Legendary, Mythic and Exalted towers may stand on the field at once. What do stars do? Each star makes a tower strike 25 percent harder in every later run, up to 15. Away from the game What happens if I leave mid-run? The tower holds. The wave does not move, so you do not come back to a lost run. See Research and time away . Does research keep running? Yes, even when the game is closed. Challenges What are Trials? Challenge runs with special rules. They open after three recasts. See Trials . What is the Daily Valley? A small seeded run that is the same for everyone on a given day. See Daily Valley and the Peal . What is the Peal? A fortnightly competition: a separate world, groups of 100, best wave wins, no chat. Does the Peal or the Daily Valley affect my main game? Only through small Bell-metal thank-yous. Their own upgrades stay in their own worlds. The world Who is Tamsin Hale? The bell-founder who kept the bell tower before you, and left you her notebook. See The story (spoilers). What does the moth do? It settles by one tower at a time, and that tower strikes truer. See The lantern moth . More in the glossary . Previous The story Next Glossary

s: The words of the valley, from Bell-metal and Hindsight to the Toll and the Roll.
x: Home The Last Bell Reference Glossary Glossary The words of the valley, from Bell-metal and Hindsight to the Toll and the Roll. Updated 11 November 2026 The bell tower: the centre of every term below. Term Meaning Bell-metal What a recast melts a run into. Buys Foundry upgrades, tower stars and research. Kept for good. Bell tower The tower in the middle of the field. If its mainspring runs down, the run ends. Brass, Fog, Harvest, Rust Four twists that change a whole valley. Call early Bringing the next wave immediately, for bonus Parts. Casing A wind-up's armour plates; each strike loses a little to it. Charge One use of the bell's rewind. See Rewind . Clock face The bell tower's clock, marking the hour every ten waves. See The clock face . Crew A woken wind-up placed in a tower, adding its strength. See Crew and the Roll . Daily Valley The seeded run that is the same for everyone each day. Echoes The faint trails left by an erased minute after a rewind. Family Bell, Spring, Weight, Air, Light, Oil or Time: the group a tower belongs to. Final form The two choices at tower level 10. Foundry Where Bell-metal is spent on upgrades, stars and research. Hindsight The strike bonus from replaying a minute: 10 percent each time, up to 30. Keeper You. Mainspring The bell tower's health. Mend What happens when a wind-up is stopped: the Rust falls away and it drops Parts. Moth The lantern moth that settles by one tower at a time. See The lantern moth . Open Field The roadless maze valley. See The Open Field . Pads The stone plots you build towers on. Parts What mended wind-ups drop; spent in a run, not kept. Peal The fortnightly competition. Recast Ending a run to turn it into Bell-metal. Roll The record of every wind-up that has woken and joined. Rust What has got into the wind-ups' springs. Stars Permanent levels for each tower, bought with Bell-metal. Tamsin Hale The bell-founder who kept the tower before you. Toll The great boss at midnight. See Wardens and Tolls . Trial A challenge run with special rules. See Trials . Twist A rule that changes a run, such as Fog. Warden The mini-boss that arrives each hour. Wind-up A clockwork foe. See The wind-ups .
