x: Home The Last Bell Reference From the same world From the same world Where the valley of stopped clocks sits in the Evenwold, and how the other games touch it. Updated 16 November 2026 On this page Your corner of the world The lantern moth Resets with a reason Four different bells The other games The Last Bell happens in the Evenwold , the country every BlairsLab game is set in. You don't need any of it to play. It's here if you're curious. Your corner of the world Here, every clock in the valley stopped on the same evening except the bell in one small stone tower. Places in the Evenwold stop for different reasons. Some are held on purpose and some just ran down. The Rust gathers where time has been left alone. See The story and Wind-ups . The lantern moth The moth is the one creature in every BlairsLab game. Here it settles on one of your towers to make it truer, and it is the one thing that stays put when the bell rewinds. It is never a weapon and never suffers because you were away. Resets with a reason Here the reset is Rewind the minute , where the bell rings backwards. In other games it is a Fold, or a Rewind of a hive. Four different bells Bells turn up across the games, and there are four different ones. The other games Hivewright : wake a hive of clockwork insects and climb a stopped tower. The Last Second Workshop : mend and build in Meridia, held at the last second. The Lamplighter : light the road, survive the Rust (closed testing). The Belfry Gun : hold a hill town's wall (in testing). The Roads Between : a story of stopped towns (closed testing). Start at the Evenwold for the shared rules. Previous Glossary

s: An idle game about building machines inside the one second before midnight, and getting a frozen city home.
x: The Last Second Workshop is an idle and incremental game for your phone. You look after a clockmaker's workshop in the city of Meridia, where time has stopped one second before midnight. You catch moments of time, build machines that turn them into more, and work towards getting the city moving again. Meridia at night: every clock agrees on the same second. Why people stay A workshop you design. Twelve kinds of machine sit on rings of sockets. Where you put them and how you route them into each other makes a big difference to output. A prestige system with choices. When your workshop is ready you Fold it, rebuild under a new law of time, and keep your permanent upgrades. A story that arrives as you grow. Transmissions from a signal operator, a courier and a missing clockmaker come in as you progress. See the story so far . No pressure. Your workshop keeps producing while you are away, and there are no timers that punish you. Read offline progress . Where to begin If you want to... Read Understand the premise The held second Play your first ten minutes well Getting started Know what each machine does Machines Grow faster Tips for faster progress Look something up FAQ and Glossary The shape of the game Catch the pulse on the central clock to gather Moments, and let your Splitters gather them for you. Upgrade and build machines, open new sockets, and route machines into chains. Keep the board stable. Too much work for the board to bear slows every machine. See load and stability . Fold once you have earned enough, collect Chronons, and spend them on permanent research . Explore new laws of time: Forward, Looping and Branching , optional Trials , and the places in the atlas of Meridia . Note: Pages with later regions and the ending are marked as spoilers, so you can read everything else freely. The game is free to play on Google Play, runs fully offline, and is available in twelve languages. Nothing you might buy is needed to finish the story.

s: The premise, the opening pages, and the first people and creatures you meet in a city stopped at 23:59:59.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Start here The held second The held second The premise, the opening pages, and the first people and creatures you meet in a city stopped at 23:59:59. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page A parcel from tomorrow The workshop inside the second The first night The first voices Every game of The Last Second Workshop begins at the same moment: 23:59:59 . The rain stopped before it reached the pavement. Across the city of Meridia, every clock agreed on the same impossible second. The last train hung between two stations. Someone was still waving from a window. Wren Street: the rain hangs in the air, waiting. A parcel from tomorrow Your workshop is at the end of Wren Street. A parcel is waiting on the step, dry under the hanging rain. Inside it are a broken escapement, a brass key and a letter dated tomorrow. The parcel: an escapement, a key and a letter. The handwriting is Iona's. She was your teacher and has been missing for seven years. The letter reads: "I did not stop the city to keep it forever. I stopped it because we had not finished getting everyone home. If you can hear the ticking, there is still a way through. Keep what matters. Let the rest change." On the back is a map of Meridia with six districts around an empty circle and your workshop drawn in the middle. One more line shows up only when you hold the paper near the clock: "Start small. A second is a place somebody can stand." The workshop inside the second One clock on your bench still moves, and that is where the game starts. You catch its pulse to gather Moments , and your first Splitter gathers them for you. Moments buy machines, machines make more Moments, and the workshop grows outward in rings. Once it has grown as far as it usefully can, you take it apart on purpose and rebuild it. That is a Fold . You can't fail, and stepping away costs you nothing. The game's own opening says there is no rush to learn everything. Your workshop: three rings of sockets, one small mechanism ticking at the centre. The first night The parcel is wrapped in a page of a railway timetable, the 23:58 to the coast, with Iona's sums pencilled in the margins. Your old tools are still on their hooks. The clock on the bench is the only thing in Meridia still ticking. Near dawn, if it is a dawn, a small light settles on the windowsill. It looks like a moth made of lamplight , and it doesn't flutter. It just waits. That is the lantern moth, your companion in the game. It drifts closer whenever you keep the beat of the clock. There is more on the characters page. The first voices Within your first few catches you hear a woman's voice between the clock's ticks. Mara Vale is a signal operator in a box beside a train that has not moved in seven years. "If anyone can hear me, do not move the train." She knows every face on the platform, and she asks you to keep answering. A little later, with four machines running, a courier called Senn turns up in your doorway with a bag of letters that never arrived. You build a path long enough for one delivery. When he comes back, his coat is wet with rain that has finished falling. The story continues as your workshop grows, one transmission at a time, in the City and Journal screen. From here: Getting started for your first ten minutes. Characters for everyone you will meet. Atlas of Meridia for the places the story visits (contains spoilers). Next Getting started

s: Your first ten minutes in the workshop, step by step, and what the game reveals as you go.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Start here Getting started Getting started Your first ten minutes in the workshop, step by step, and what the game reveals as you go. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The first steps What unlocks as you play Meet your guide Your first Fold While you are away You start straight in the workshop, and the opening prologue plays after your first few catches. A short hands-on tutorial in a separate practice workshop teaches the basics, with optional lessons for the advanced parts. You can replay the guide any time from Settings. The workshop screen: your four resources along the top, your guide below them, the ring underneath. The first steps Catch your first Moments. Tap the small clock in the centre of the board, or hold the CATCH A MOMENT button to repeat. A well-timed tap earns more. Your starting Splitter also produces automatically, so you never have to keep tapping. Upgrade your Splitter. Tap the Splitter on the inner ring. Its controls open at the bottom of the screen. Choose x1, x10, x25 or Max levels, check the price, then tap Upgrade. More levels mean more production. Make room. Tap the locked socket next to your Splitter and buy it with Moments. Core sockets are permanent, and they survive every Fold. Then tap an empty socket and install another machine. Connect your machines. Tap a machine, choose Route from here, and tap another. Arrows show the direction. See rings and routes . Watch the load. Above the clock you will see Load and a limit. Stay at or under the limit and every machine runs at full speed. See load and stability . What unlocks as you play Screens unlock as you progress, and the game points out each new one as it opens: At the start you see only the Workshop, with the catch button and your Splitter. Soon after, you can unlock more sockets. A first message waits in City and Journal. Next, routes unlock, and Discoveries appear under More. Then Research and machine modifications open. After two discoveries, try the Efficient modification. Later, expanded rings, saved layouts and the Layouts screen become available. Finally the Fold screen previews your first Fold, with a target of 2.5 million Moments earned in a run . Spending Moments does not reduce that total. Meet your guide Characters give you short goals, like catching ten Moments by hand, raising a Splitter to level 10 or running two machines. Each finished goal can be claimed for a reward worth about two minutes of your current production, so it stays useful at every stage. See characters . Your first Fold When you reach 2.5 million Moments earned in a single run, the Fold screen offers your first Fold. It shows exactly what you will keep and what resets before you confirm. Read Folds first, since the whole game builds around it. Tip: You do not need to understand everything in your first session. The game explains each system when it unlocks, and nothing you do early on can lock you out of later content. While you are away Close the game whenever you like. Your workshop keeps producing for up to four hours at full rate, and it shows you what it earned when you return. More in offline progress . For faster progress once you have the basics, go to tips for faster progress . Previous The held second Next Tips for faster progress

s: How Moments, Precision, Chronons and Prisms fit together, and how one run turns into the next.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems The core loop The core loop How Moments, Precision, Chronons and Prisms fit together, and how one run turns into the next. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The short loop: inside a run The long loop: across runs The four resources Nothing is lost for spending What pushes you forward Pace The game has two loops. A short one happens inside a run, and a long one carries over between runs. The short loop: inside a run Catch and produce. Tapping gathers Moments. Splitters make them automatically. Spend. Moments buy machine levels, new machines, sockets and ring expansions. Connect. Routes make one machine strengthen another. Balance. Load must stay within capacity, or efficiency falls. Repeat with a bigger workshop. The long loop: across runs When a run has earned enough, you Fold . The workshop is cleared, you receive Chronons , and you rebuild under a law of time of your choice. Chronons buy permanent research , which makes every later run faster and lets you get further each time. The four resources Resource Colour on screen What it does Does it reset on a Fold? Moments Gold The main currency. Spend it on machines, levels, sockets and rings. Yes Precision Cyan Made by Archives. Buys run research and fuels Phase Shifters. Yes Chronons Violet Earned by Folding. Buys permanent research and unlocks laws of time. No Prisms Pink A gem currency earned from discoveries, Trials and daily tasks. No Nothing is lost for spending Spending Moments does not reduce your run total. The Fold target counts what you earned in the run, whatever you are holding now. The game repeats this a few times because new players worry about it. What pushes you forward Discoveries record milestones such as your first thousand Moments or your first Fold. They unlock blueprints and machine modifications. See discoveries and experiments . The story opens chapters as you reach milestones. See atlas of Meridia . Optional goals such as Trials and daily tasks are there when you want a challenge. Pace There is no failure state, and you can't lose progress by playing it wrong. The game suggests you Fold when the climb slows . Later Folds ask for more each time but pay more too. The Folds page covers when to do it. Tip: If you only have a minute, tap a few times, spend Moments on the cheapest upgrade and close the game. Previous Tips for faster progress Next Catching Moments

s: Practical, rule-backed advice for the early game, the mid game and every Fold.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Start here Tips for faster progress Tips for faster progress Practical, rule-backed advice for the early game, the mid game and every Fold. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Your first session Building well Choosing when to Fold When you are away For the active player For the curious None of this is required. It all comes from how the game's rules work. Your first session Tap early, tap well. A standard catch is worth at least 1 Moment, and a perfect catch doubles it. When your production is small, your hands are a big share of your income. See catching Moments . Upgrade your first Splitter a few times before building more. A Splitter's output is its level, multiplied by 1.5 for every 25 levels , so levels pay back well. Claim your guide's goals. Each claim pays about two minutes of your current production, with a minimum of 50 Moments. See characters . Buy core sockets early. They cost 25, 100, 300, 750, 1,500, 3,000 and 6,000 Moments in order, and they are permanent across Folds . Building well Chain Splitters clockwise in Forward Time. Each Splitter stage feeding a machine gives it +8%, up to +40%. See rings and routes . Add Lenses to your strongest Splitter. Each Lens gives up to +50% and Lenses combined cap at +100%. Level in steps of 25. Each full 25 levels multiplies a Splitter's output by 1.5. Using the x25 button gets you there efficiently. Watch Load, not just production. If Load exceeds capacity, every machine slows. Add an Escapement before another producer. See load and stability . Use Efficient and Overclocked on purpose. Efficient frees capacity, Overclocked uses it for more output. See modifications and blueprints . Save a layout once you have a design you like, so rebuilding after a Fold is quick and the game shows you the cost. Up to twelve layouts can be saved. Choosing when to Fold Do not hoard Moments. Spending never reduces what the run has earned, so spend as soon as you can afford something good. Fold when the climb slows. Chronons grow fastest up to the run's peak, then more slowly. Waiting far beyond the peak invites Strain, which makes costs rise. See Folds . Spend Chronons on Temporal yield first. It multiplies all Moment production, and it is the game's own recommendation. See research . Spread research across lines. Each rank costs double the last, so a few ranks of several lines usually beat many ranks of one. When you are away Spend before you leave. Your workshop earns for up to four hours at its full rate, so a stronger workshop earns more while you are away. Check Load before closing the game. An overloaded board wastes your offline hours. Take Long memory if you often stay away more than four hours. It extends the limit by 2.5 hours per rank, up to 24 hours. See offline progress . Do not chase Golden seconds offline. They pass while you are away, so claim them when you are playing. For the active player Aim for full Rhythm. Ten perfect taps in a row grows your Rhythm streak, fills Resonance faster, and meets the lantern moth. Streak bursts pay well. 10 perfect taps in a row pays 5 seconds of production, 25 pays 15, and every 50 pays 30. Buy Steady Hands, Surge Coil and Golden Instinct for a run that is heavy on tapping. They reset on a Fold, so buy them early. Finish daily tasks that match what you were doing anyway. See daily tasks . For the curious Try each temporal law once. Each changes how you build. See temporal laws . Try a Trial after your third Fold. They are

s: Tapping, Rhythm, Surges, Golden seconds, Resonance and the catch upgrades, explained with their real numbers.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Catching Moments Catching Moments Tapping, Rhythm, Surges, Golden seconds, Resonance and the catch upgrades, explained with their real numbers. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The basic catch Rhythm Streak bursts Surges Golden seconds Resonance Catch upgrades Permanent catch research The big clock at the centre of the workshop is what you tap. Tapping is optional, but it pays well, especially early in a run. The basic catch Tap the clock's centre pulse, or hold the CATCH A MOMENT button to repeat. A standard catch pays 10% of your passive production per second , with a minimum of 1 Moment, so the first taps still count for something. A perfect catch, timed to the pulse, pays double. You can catch at most four times a second. Holding the button gives the standard reward every time, but it never triggers the bonuses below. Those need deliberate taps. Rhythm Every consecutive perfect tap builds a Rhythm streak, adding +5% to each catch. The streak can grow to 10 taps by default. An off-beat tap, or a pause longer than three seconds, breaks it. Reaching full Rhythm is also how you meet the lantern moth . Streak bursts Long unbroken runs of perfect taps pay out extra in seconds of your production: Perfect taps in a row Bonus 10 5 seconds of production 25 15 seconds of production 50, and every 50 after 30 seconds of production Surges Every 30 catches, a Surge releases 10 seconds of your production at once. Golden seconds Roughly every 150 to 300 seconds, a Golden second appears on the clock for about 8 seconds. Tap during it and you receive 60 seconds of your production. If you are away, Golden seconds pass unclaimed. Resonance Each perfect tap fills a Resonance meter, and it fills faster the longer your Rhythm streak. When the meter is full, your passive production is lifted by 25% for 30 seconds . Boosts do not stack, so Resonance adds nothing while a stronger boost is already running. Catch upgrades Catch upgrades are bought with Moments from the Workshop and reset when you Fold , like machine levels. Upgrade Effect Ranks Steady Hands +15% Moments from every tapped catch 20 Long Rhythm Rhythm can grow 2 taps longer, for +10% more maximum bonus 5 Surge Coil Surges arrive 3 catches sooner 5 Golden Instinct Golden seconds appear 10% sooner and last 1 second longer 5 Buying any catch upgrade is also the moth's first goal for you. Permanent catch research Two permanent research lines help your hands: Sensitive hands adds 10% to catch rewards per rank, and Automatic hands unlocks a toggle for one standard automatic catch per second. In each run, you can also buy a Precision-funded Catch window upgrade that widens the perfect-catch window by 10 milliseconds per rank. Tip: A Conductor machine adds a capped bonus to active catches without needing a route. See machines . Note: Tapping matters most early. Once your workshop produces a lot per second, your catches are a small share of the total, and many players just check in now and then. See tips . Previous The core loop Next Machines

s: All twelve machines, what each does, when it unlocks, and how to use it well.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Machines Machines All twelve machines, what each does, when it unlocks, and how to use it well. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The twelve machines The numbers behind output Producers, supporters and keepers Phases Weights and load Building well Your workshop has twelve kinds of machine. Each unlocks once your lifetime Moments reach a threshold. Unlocks are permanent and stay after a Fold. A machine's install cost is the price of placing it at level 1. After that you buy levels, and every level costs 17% more than the last. The twelve machines Machine Unlocks at (lifetime Moments) What it does Splitter Start Produces Moments. Route Splitters clockwise to build a production chain. Lens 100 Route it to a producer for +5% plus 1% per square root of its level, up to +50% each. Together, lenses cap at +100%. Escapement 200 Adds 3 plus 0.2 per level to this board's stability capacity. Archive 300 Produces Precision for run research and for Phase Shifter fuel. Bridge 500 Has three outgoing routes and lets rings connect away from the quarter points. Conductor 800 Adds a capped bonus to active catches. No route needed. Reservoir 1,500 Route a Splitter into it. It stores 20% of that Splitter's output and releases it every 30 seconds with a level bonus. Synchroniser 2,500 Route it to a producer with the same phase for +15%, up to +50% combined. Phase Shifter 4,000 When enabled, spends Precision every 30 seconds to rotate its target's phase by one. Echo Chamber 6,000 Route a Splitter into it. It repeats a fraction of that Splitter's unmodified base output. Echoes cannot echo. Anchor 10,000 Preserves some of a loop's resonance when you change the circuit. Combined retention caps at 75%. Observatory 15,000 Advances experiments and earns Precision. The numbers behind output A Splitter makes its level in Moments per second, multiplied by 1.5 for every full 25 levels . Levels 25 and 50 are worth aiming for. An Archive works the same way for Precision, at 0.02 per level, with a 1.4 multiplier for every 25 levels. Machine levels top out at one million. Producers, supporters and keepers Machines fall into three roles: Producers make resources: Splitters (Moments), Echo Chambers (extra Moments), Archives (Precision) and Observatories. Supporters strengthen what they are routed to: Lens, Synchroniser, Phase Shifter, Reservoir, Echo Chamber, Conductor. Keepers protect the board: Escapement (capacity), Anchor (loop resonance), Bridge (wiring). Phases Every machine has a phase, from 0 to 3. A Synchroniser only helps a producer on the same phase. A Phase Shifter spends Precision to rotate a target's phase, and you can switch it on and off. If you are not using Synchronisers, you can ignore phases entirely. Weights and load Most machines count as 1 toward your board's load. Escapements, Bridges and Anchors count as half. The heavier a machine's level, the more load it adds. See load and stability . Building well Early on, more Splitters in a chain beat everything else. See rings and routes . Add a Lens to a strong Splitter before you add a fourth or fifth one. Once the board is straining, install an Escapement instead of another producer. Add an Archive when you want run research. See research . Each machine can also carry one modification . Tip: Not sure what a machine is for? Tap it on the ring and read its card. It always shows its own description and cost before you buy. Previous Catching Moments Next Rings, sockets

s: How the three rings of sockets work, how to expand them, and the rules for routing one machine into another.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Rings, sockets and routes Rings, sockets and routes How the three rings of sockets work, how to expand them, and the rules for routing one machine into another. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The three rings Costs Routing The rules What routes do Layouts Your workshop is a brass instrument with rings of numbered sockets around a central clock. Machines sit in sockets, and routes carry one machine's output to another. The three rings Ring Sockets How you get it Core Up to 8 Buy sockets one at a time, in order, with Moments. Orbital 12 Expand the branch once you can afford it. Horizon 16 Expand again after the Orbital ring. That is 36 sockets on a single board. Tap Core, Orbital or Horizon to inspect one ring more clearly, and pinch to zoom in when you are planning a layout. Costs Core sockets cost, in order: 25, 100, 300, 750, 1,500, 3,000 and 6,000 Moments. They are permanent and survive every Fold. Expanding to the Orbital ring costs 2,500 Moments, and the Horizon ring costs 25,000. Rings reset when you Fold. Opening the Orbital ring is one of the early discoveries, and it is how you meet the courier Senn properly. See characters . Routing To connect machines, tap one, choose Route from here , then tap the destination. The menu hides while you choose, and arrows show the direction. The rules Each machine has one output . A Bridge has three. In Forward and Branching Time, a route must point forward : to a later socket clockwise, or out to an outer ring. You cannot route backwards. In Looping Time , routes may go in any direction, including back to where they started. Different rings connect only at their quarter points : the 12, 3, 6 and 9 o'clock sockets. A Bridge removes that limit. In Branching Time, routes stay within one branch. The branches combine through their own bonus. See temporal laws . If a route is not allowed, the game tells you why. What routes do In Forward Time the receiving machine gains +8% output for every Splitter stage feeding into it, up to +40% at five stages . The sender keeps all of its own output, so chaining costs you nothing. Other machines use routes differently: A Lens , Synchroniser or Phase Shifter affects the machine it is routed to . A Reservoir or Echo Chamber works on the Splitter routed into it. A Conductor needs no route at all. Layouts Once a design works, you can save it as a layout, up to twelve of them. After a Fold, apply the layout and the game tells you which machines are missing and what they cost. Layouts load positions, routes, modifications and phases, but not levels, currency or stored production. A layout only applies to the same temporal law and blueprint it was saved under. See folds . Core, Orbital and Horizon: three rings, thirty-six sockets. Tip: Build the chain around the ring clockwise, then place Lenses and Reservoirs on sockets that sit just after your strongest Splitters. See also load and stability . Previous Machines Next Load and stability

s: Why a busy board slows down, how to read the Load meter, and the ways to give your workshop room to breathe.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Load and stability Load and stability Why a busy board slows down, how to read the Load meter, and the ways to give your workshop room to breathe. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page What the numbers mean How load is counted Raising capacity How big is the penalty? Strain: when a long run gets heavy Reading the situation Above the clock, you will see a Load readout such as Load 8.2 / 8.0 . Once your workshop gets busy, this is the number to watch. What the numbers mean Load is how hard your machines are working the board. Every machine adds to it, and higher levels add more. Capacity is how much the board can bear. It starts at 8 . Efficiency is how well your machines run. At or under capacity it is 100%. If Load exceeds capacity, every machine gives a little less. Nothing breaks and nothing is lost, but all the machines run slower together. The game's own wording is: more machines are not always better. How load is counted Each machine adds a weight, multiplied by a factor that grows as it levels up (2% per level). Escapements, Bridges and Anchors count as half-weight machines. Everything else counts as one. The Load meter responds to modifications too: Efficient reduces a machine's load by 30%. Overclocked makes a machine produce 30% more, but adds 50% more load. See modifications and blueprints . Raising capacity Source Effect Escapement machines +3 plus 0.2 per level, each Stable foundations research +2 per rank, permanent Capacity run research +2 per rank, this run only An Escapement is the usual answer to a straining board. Its capacity rises as you level it. How big is the penalty? When load goes over capacity, efficiency falls as the overshoot grows. If you are at 1.5 times capacity, efficiency is 80%. The slope is gradual, but it adds up when you are far over. Strain: when a long run gets heavy A separate effect called Strain affects very long runs. Once a run has earned well past its peak point, which is twice the point where Chronon gains start to slow, machine costs begin to rise. Strain resets with every Fold. It is the game's way of telling you the climb has slowed and a Fold is due. See folds . Reading the situation The Load chip turns amber and shows a warning mark when you are over. Tap Load above the ring and the game offers help. Some story goals and one of the Trials care about load too. Tip: If you are only slightly over capacity, a few extra levels on an Escapement are cheaper than losing efficiency across the board. Warning: Adding another Splitter is not always an improvement. If it pushes you far over capacity, it can lower your total output. Previous Rings, sockets and routes Next Research

s: Permanent research bought with Chronons, run research bought with Precision, and which upgrades to take first.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Research Research Permanent research bought with Chronons, run research bought with Precision, and which upgrades to take first. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Permanent research (Chronons) What to take first Run research (Precision) Catch upgrades Where it fits There are two kinds of research. They share the Research tab but work differently. Permanent research (Chronons) Chronons come from Folding, and permanent research survives every Fold . Each rank costs double the one before it, starting from the base cost in the table. Research Effect per rank Ranks First rank costs Temporal yield +25% Moment production 20 1 Chronon Stable foundations +2 capacity per board 10 1 Long memory +2.5 offline hours, from 4 hours up to 24 8 1 Sensitive hands +10% catch rewards 10 1 Perfect optics +10% Lens strength, keeping each Lens cap 5 2 Fine measurement +10% Precision production 10 1 Efficient assembly Machine installation and upgrades cost 4% less 5 2 Resonant memory Loops warm up 10% faster (needs Looping Time) 5 2 Parallel thought +5% convergence bonus (needs Branching Time) 5 3 Deep reserves +2% Reservoir release bonus 5 2 Automatic hands Unlocks a toggle for one standard automatic catch per second 1 2 Head start Start each Fold with 25 Moments 5 1 Research cards explain each benefit before you buy. What to take first The game's own guide suggests Temporal yield first, since it multiplies everything. After that it depends on what is holding you back: Boards straining under load: Stable foundations . Long absences: Long memory . See offline progress . Wanting an easier early run: Efficient assembly and Head start . Interested in the other laws of time: Resonant memory and Parallel thought . See temporal laws . Tip: Because each rank doubles in price, spreading Chronons across several research lines is often better than pushing one line to its limit. Run research (Precision) Run research is bought with Precision from your Archives and resets when you Fold . There are three lines, and each rank costs 10 Precision doubled for every rank already bought. Run research Effect per rank Ranks Production +10% production 20 Capacity +2 capacity per board 20 Catch window +10 milliseconds to the perfect-catch window 8 Early in a run, an Archive and a few ranks of Production and Capacity pay for themselves quickly. Later on, your Precision keeps accumulating while you are away. Catch upgrades A third kind of upgrade is bought with Moments: the catch upgrades . These also reset on Fold. Where it fits Permanent research carries over every Fold, so your next run starts with higher production, a bigger offline allowance and cheaper machines. You reach the target sooner and Fold for more. See Folds . Previous Load and stability Next Modifications and blueprints

s: The five machine modifications and six workshop blueprints, with when each unlocks and what it trades off.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Modifications and blueprints Modifications and blueprints The five machine modifications and six workshop blueprints, with when each unlocks and what it trades off. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Modifications Choosing between them Blueprints Picking a blueprint Where to see them Two systems let you tailor your workshop: modifications change a single machine, and blueprints change the whole board for a run. Both are unlocked by discoveries . Modifications Each machine can carry one modification, shown as a short code beside its level badge. You can change them freely, apart from a short cooldown after a change. Modification Discoveries needed Effect Efficient 2 30% less load. Overclocked 4 +30% output, +50% load. Harmonic 6 Stronger synchronisation. Patient 8 +25% after 60 seconds unchanged. Responsive 10 +25% for 5 seconds after you catch a pulse. Choosing between them Efficient suits a board near its limit. Overclocked is for boards with spare capacity, where you want more output. Harmonic only matters on machines you have Synchronisers feeding. Patient is for set-and-forget workshops. Do not rearrange and it pays +25%. Responsive suits active play, with a short lift after every catch. Note: Patient counts from the last time that machine was changed, so swapping modifications on it every few minutes wastes its bonus. The Purist Trial asks you to Fold without ever giving a machine a modification. Blueprints At each Fold you choose a blueprint , a strategic bonus paired with a constraint that shapes the whole run. Blueprint Discoveries needed What it does Clockmaker's Bench 0 Balanced output and capacity. Pendulum Foundry 3 +25% Moments; +15% load; base capacity of 6 instead of 8. Prism Array 6 +50% Lens strength; -15% Moments; at most half a ring occupied by Splitters. Echo Vault 9 +50% Reservoir release bonus; -10% immediate Moments. Twin Observatory 12 +50% Precision and experiment work; -20% Moments. Event Horizon Engine 16 +30% Moments at 80% to 100% load; twice the usual overload penalty. Picking a blueprint The Bench is the safe default and a good choice while you learn. The Pendulum Foundry is strong early, since a 25% boost outweighs the capacity cost if you tend your Escapements. The Prism Array wants plenty of Lenses and rewards a few strong Splitters over many. The Echo Vault suits boards built around Reservoirs. The Twin Observatory is a research-focused run: more Precision, fewer Moments. The Event Horizon Engine is the risky one. It pays out while load sits between 80% and 100% of capacity, and the penalty beyond that is twice the usual. Your blueprint is part of the layout you save, and layouts only apply under the blueprint they were saved with. See rings and routes . Where to see them You choose the blueprint on the Fold screen, together with the temporal law for your next run. See Folds and temporal laws . Previous Research Next Folds

s: The prestige system explained. When to Fold, what resets, what you keep, how Chronons are earned and how each Fold changes the next run.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Folds Folds The prestige system explained. When to Fold, what resets, what you keep, how Chronons are earned and how each Fold changes the next run. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Your first Fold What you keep and what you reset How Chronons are earned When to Fold Each Fold raises the bar Choosing your next run Story and Folds A Fold is the game's prestige system. You take your finished workshop apart on purpose, receive Chronons , and rebuild under a new law of time. In the story's own words, the workshop "comes apart without breaking. Every screw returns to the bench; every lesson remains in your hands." Your first Fold Your first Fold becomes possible at 2.5 million Moments earned in a single run , and it pays your first Chronon. The Fold tab shows your target, the reward you would receive right now, and what resets, before you confirm anything. What you keep and what you reset You keep You reset Chronons Moments and Precision Permanent research Machines and their levels Discoveries and saved layouts Run research and rings Core sockets and Prisms Catch upgrades Story progress, characters met Rhythm, Surge and Golden timers After a Fold you start again with a single Splitter on each board, in the law and blueprint you chose. If you took Head start research, you also begin with a small stock of Moments. How Chronons are earned The more Moments you earned in the run, the more Chronons you receive, but the curve changes shape: Up to a peak point , Chronons grow fast , rising with the square of your Moments. Past the peak, gains slow down but never stop. On a first run the peak is about 7.9 million Moments. It rises with every Chronon you hold, so it keeps moving up as you progress. The game reminds you of this on the screen: Chronons grow fastest until a certain number of run-earned Moments, then more slowly. Fold when the climb slows. When to Fold Fold around the peak or shortly after. Waiting much longer than that pays only a little more, and if you run well past it, Strain makes machine costs climb. See load and stability . Folding early isn't punished, but you can't farm it either, since every Chronon raises the peak equally however you earned it. Tip: Fold when your Moments per second stops climbing noticeably. Your next run will start faster because of what you just earned. Each Fold raises the bar Because your peak rises with your lifetime Chronons, the target for each new Fold grows too. In return, your permanent research makes every run faster, so reaching the new target takes less effort than the last one did. Choosing your next run On the Fold screen you choose: A temporal law : Forward, Looping or Branching. See temporal laws . Looping unlocks at 15 lifetime Chronons and Branching at 60 . The Fold you are about to take counts toward those numbers. A blueprint . See modifications and blueprints . Optionally, after your third Fold, a Trial . See trials . Story and Folds Folding is tied to the story. The first Fold introduces the Counter, Meridia's timekeeper. Further transmissions arrive at later Folds, including at your seventh and eighteenth. See characters . Note: Spending Moments does not reduce your run total, so you never need to hoard Moments to reach the target. Spend freely. Previous Modifications and blueprints Next Temporal laws

s: Forward, Looping and Branching Time, how each one changes the way machines connect, and how to build for each.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Temporal laws Temporal laws Forward, Looping and Branching Time, how each one changes the way machines connect, and how to build for each. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Forward Time Looping Time Branching Time Which should I pick? Every time you Fold , you choose the temporal law your next run follows. The law decides how routes behave and what kind of workshop is rewarded. Your current law and blueprint are shown above the ring, for example "Looping Time - Clockmaker's Bench". Law Unlocks at The idea Forward Time Start Long clockwise chains. Looping Time 15 lifetime Chronons Closed circuits that build resonance. Branching Time 60 lifetime Chronons Two boards working in balance. The Fold you are about to take counts toward these totals, so the Fold screen tells you if a law will be available. Forward Time Routes must point forward: to a later socket clockwise, or out to an outer ring. Each Splitter feeding a machine gives it +8% output, up to +40% at five stages . The sender keeps its own output. Build one long clockwise chain of Splitters, then add Lenses and Reservoirs around it. Routes can never form a cycle. Looping Time Routes may go in any direction, so you can close a circuit. Machines in a closed circuit build resonance , rising towards +75% over a few minutes (the warm-up has a time constant of 90 seconds). Looping Time: routes may travel in any direction, so circuits can close. Changing a circuit resets its resonance, so settle your layout first and leave it alone. Anchor machines keep part of the resonance when you change a loop. Combined retention is capped at 75%. Resonant memory research makes loops warm up 10% faster per rank. Branching Time Your workshop is split into two boards , Branch A and Branch B, each with its own Splitter, rings and load. Routes stay inside one branch, and there is no chain bonus in this law. Use routes for support machines. The two boards earn a convergence bonus when their production is balanced, so the aim is to keep both boards strong and similar. Parallel thought research strengthens that bonus. Each board has its own capacity and its own load, so check both. A selector on the workshop switches between Branch A and Branch B. Which should I pick? Learning the ropes: Forward Time, always. Interested in clever circuits: Looping Time, once available. Patient planners who enjoy balancing two boards: Branching Time. Each law has its own matching challenge on the Experiment Board. See discoveries and experiments , and you can save a layout per law. Layouts only apply to the law they were saved under. Tip: If a run feels stuck in one law, try a different one at your next Fold. Your Chronons, research and discoveries carry over, and only the way machines connect changes. Previous Folds Next Discoveries and experiments

s: All 24 discoveries and how to earn them, plus the four Experiment Board challenges.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Discoveries and experiments Discoveries and experiments All 24 discoveries and how to earn them, plus the four Experiment Board challenges. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The full list Easy ones for early on Harder ones The Experiment Board Discoveries are milestones the game records as you play. There are 24 , they are found under More , and they never expire or reset. Each one can be collected for a small Prism reward. The number you have found unlocks blueprints and modifications , and a few open story chapters. The full list Group Discoveries Moments earned (lifetime) First hundred; A thousand moments; Ten thousand moments; A hundred thousand; Million moments; Billion moments Machines installed Two machines; Four machines; Eight machines; Sixteen machines Kinds of machine Three disciplines; Six disciplines; Nine disciplines; All twelve disciplines Precision First Precision; Precision reserve: 100 Catches Ten catches; One hundred catches Laws A living circuit (a closed loop in Looping Time); Parallel clocks (a Splitter on the second branch in Branching Time) Folds First Fold; Five Folds Expansion Orbital expansion; Horizon expansion "Machines installed" and "kinds of machine" both count what is in your workshop at one time. Once a discovery is recorded, it is yours for good, even after a Fold clears the board. Easy ones for early on Tap ten times to get Ten catches . Install a second Splitter for Two machines . Build an Archive for First Precision . Open the Orbital ring for Orbital expansion . It also introduces a new character. Harder ones All twelve disciplines needs one of every machine kind installed together, so plan sockets for it. Horizon expansion needs the third ring on a board. A living circuit and Parallel clocks need you to choose those laws at a Fold. The Experiment Board Alongside your discoveries under More, an Experiment Board offers four challenges. Each asks you to hold a condition for 120 uninterrupted seconds , and then you claim 50 Precision . You can repeat any of them. Experiment The challenge Quiet engineering Run at least four machines without any Escapement and without overload. Clockwise cascade In Forward Time, keep a chain with three upstream Splitter stages. Closed eternity In Looping Time, keep at least six machines in closed circuits. Perfect counterparts In Branching Time, keep both branches' production within 10% of each other. The Looping and Branching experiments stay hidden until you can choose those laws. Experiments are optional. Observatory machines also advance experiments and earn Precision. See machines . Tip: The Experiment Board is a good warm-up for the Trials , which ask for similar restraint across a whole run. Previous Temporal laws Next Trials of the Held Second

s: Ten optional rules you can take on for one run, earn a seal for, and master for up to three stars each.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Trials of the Held Second Trials of the Held Second Ten optional rules you can take on for one run, earn a seal for, and master for up to three stars each. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page How Trials work Stars The ten Trials A voice for each seal Tips for Trials After three Folds , the Fold screen offers an optional extra: a Trial . You pick one rule to follow for the next run. Fold again while the rule still holds and you earn that Trial's seal . The Single Ring Trial: the board says which Trial is active just under the law and blueprint. How Trials work A seal is only recognition. It does not change production, and you never need a Trial. Breaking the rule ends the Trial and only the Trial. Your run carries on normally. The rule is checked after every action and every step of the simulation, so time away is treated the same as time at the bench. Trials never expire or rotate. Take them whenever you like. Stars A Fold under the rule that pays enough Chronons earns a star . Each Trial has its own goal, and the second star needs 1.5 times the goal and the third needs twice the goal. Each star pays once, in a small reward of Prisms and, for the higher stars, stored time skips. It never pays production or Chronons. You can replay a Trial to earn more stars. The ten Trials Trial The rule Chronons for the first star Single Ring Fold without opening a second ring. Core sockets are fine. 4 Steady State Fold without the board ever going over capacity. 4 Lone Splitter Never more than one Splitter on a board. 5 Minimalist Never more than four machines installed at once. 3 Purist Fold without giving any machine a modification. 4 Clear Glass Fold without ever installing a Lens. 5 Unbraced Fold without ever installing an Escapement. 4 Short Wiring Never more than three routes at once. 4 Two Rings Fold without opening a third ring on any board. 5 Few Kinds Never more than three kinds of machine installed at once. 3 The second and third stars need those goals multiplied by 1.5 and 2, rounded up. For example, Single Ring wants 4, 6 and 8 Chronons. A voice for each seal Each Trial ends with a comment from Iona or Mara. For Single Ring, Iona says: "One ring, and you made it sing. I will stop calling that bench too small." Tips for Trials Steady State is a good first Trial. Add an Escapement early and keep an eye on Load. See load and stability . Minimalist and Few Kinds reward upgrading a handful of machines deeply. Levels in multiples of 25 give a 1.5x multiplier to a Splitter's output. See machines . Clear Glass and Unbraced mean doing without a favourite tool, so plan for that from the start of the run. Because a Trial asks for a large Chronon payout, the stars suit a run where you let the board grow towards its peak. See Folds . Take on a Trial in a law you know well. See temporal laws . Note: If you accidentally break a Trial's rule, carry on with the run. You can try it again at your next Fold. Previous Discoveries and experiments Next Daily tasks

s: Three small tasks a day, a chest for finishing them, and why missing a day costs you nothing.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Daily tasks Daily tasks Three small tasks a day, a chest for finishing them, and why missing a day costs you nothing. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page When they appear What the tasks ask for Rewards Swapping a task What counts No streaks, no penalties Once you are past the opening, the workshop offers three small tasks a day . Each is sized to take a few minutes of normal play. They give you a reason to check in, and you can't fall behind on them. When they appear Daily tasks open after the opening phase: once you have made your first connection, or have already Folded. The practice workshop used in the tutorial never has them. A fresh set is drawn at your local midnight , from a pool of tasks that suit your stage in the game, so you are never asked for something you have not met yet. What the tasks ask for The pool covers every part of the game: tapping, perfect taps, installing machines, buying levels, making routes, earning Moments, running experiments, buying research, buying catch upgrades, applying modifications, catching a Golden second, filling Resonance, and building a Rhythm streak. As you advance, tasks ask for a little more and pay more. Targets grow a fifth per tier, rewards grow two fifths per tier, and tiers follow your lifetime Chronons. Rewards Each task pays one of three things: A stored time skip of 15 minutes or an hour. A pack of minutes of your own workshop's Moments , such as 10, 15 or 20 minutes' worth at the start. A few Prisms . Finish all three and you open the day's chest . Collect three chests in a week for a bonus. Swapping a task You get one free swap a day . A task you cannot do right now can always be swapped. What counts Progress is counted only for your own actions while the game is open . Time away, time skips and the practice workshop count for nothing. No streaks, no penalties There is no streak . If you miss a day, nothing is lost and nothing expires. The next day's tasks are drawn as normal. Tip: Pick off the tasks you were going to do anyway. Taps, upgrades and routes are part of normal play, so most tasks finish by themselves. See also: catching Moments , research , offline progress . Previous Trials of the Held Second Next Offline progress and automation

s: How your workshop keeps working while you are away, how to extend the limit, and what runs by itself.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Systems Offline progress and automation Offline progress and automation How your workshop keeps working while you are away, how to extend the limit, and what runs by itself. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Offline production What does not happen offline What runs by itself Tips for offline play The game is meant for short visits, and the workshop keeps producing while the app is closed. Offline production When you close the game, your machines keep producing at 100% of their passive rate for up to 4 hours . When you come back, the game shows a message such as "Away: +[Moments] over [time]" , and the Moments are already saved. The Long memory research adds 2.5 hours per rank, across 8 ranks, up to a 24-hour ceiling. See research . Offline time counts the same as online time, so leaving has no penalty. What does not happen offline Golden seconds appear and expire while you are away. Claim them with a tap when you are present. Catches don't happen offline, so your passive rate is what counts. Time away counts for nothing on daily tasks , which are about playing. If the game cannot verify how long you were away, it limits what it will credit. Precision from Archives and experiment work from Observatories also keep going while you are away. What runs by itself What How Splitters Make Moments automatically, always. Archives Make Precision automatically. Reservoirs Store a share of a Splitter's output and release it every 30 seconds. Phase Shifters When switched on, spend Precision every 30 seconds to rotate a target's phase. Automatic hands Permanent research that adds a toggle for one standard automatic catch per second. Automatic hands is a single-rank research costing 2 Chronons to start. Once bought, the toggle in the workshop reads "Hands on" or "Hands off". Each automatic catch is a standard catch, so keep tapping yourself when you want a perfect catch or a Rhythm streak. Tips for offline play Spend your Moments before you close the game, so the upgrades are working while you are away. Check that Load is within capacity so production is not being wasted. See load and stability . Keep your layout settled. A Patient machine pays +25% after 60 seconds untouched, which suits long absences. If you are away more than 4 hours regularly, Long memory is a strong early research pick. Note: There are no daily login streaks, and no timers that punish you for stepping away. s: Iona, Mara, Senn, the Counter and the lantern moth: who they are, when you meet them, and the goals they set.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Story and people Characters Characters Iona, Mara, Senn, the Counter and the lantern moth: who they are, when you meet them, and the goals they set. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Iona, the clockmaker Mara Vale, the signal operator Senn, the courier The Counter, Meridia's timekeeper The lantern moth Goal rewards Your guides appear as you reach milestones, and each one stays once you have met them. They give short goals along a single path through the early game. A character's goals only show once you have met them, and they never change your production. You can see everyone you have met under More , in the Characters screen. Iona, the clockmaker Iona: the clockmaker who stopped midnight. With you from the start. Iona taught you clockmaking, then vanished seven years ago. She left you a parcel, a key and a job. Her motto: "Keep what matters. Let the rest change." Her goals: catch 10 Moments by hand; raise a Splitter to level 10; unlock a second socket; run two machines; earn 1,000 lifetime Moments. Mara Vale, the signal operator Mara Vale: signal operator, still waiting for the last train. Met when you connect two machines with a route. Mara speaks through the radio from signal box three, beside a train that has not moved in seven years. She has counted every passenger and given some of them names. Her motto: "Every route you build is a way home for someone." Her goals: connect two machines; build a chain of three Splitters; reach 50 Moments per second; install an Escapement; expand to the Orbital ring. Senn, the courier Senn: a courier with a bag of undelivered letters. Met when you expand to the Orbital ring. Senn wears a patched yellow coat and carries letters that never found their door. He is dry and kind. His motto: "Bigger workshop, more letters. I'm not complaining." His goals: run eight machines; record ten discoveries; earn a million lifetime Moments; Fold for the first time. The Counter, Meridia's timekeeper The Counter: a timekeeping machine whose emblem is a ringed brass dial. Met at your first Fold. The Counter was built to make Meridia's trains run on time and was never told what the time was for. It speaks in a flat, even voice through the station loudspeaker and keeps asking questions. Its motto: "Recording. Every repetition is a new attempt." Its goals: research Temporal yield; earn 15 lifetime Chronons; close a circuit in Looping Time; record all 24 discoveries. The lantern moth The lantern moth: light between seconds. Met when you reach full Rhythm: 10 perfect taps in a row. The moth first appears in the prologue, a small light on the windowsill that waits. When you meet it properly, the game says: "Something small and bright slips out from between two seconds and settles on your clock. It stays close whenever you keep the beat." The game describes it as "light between seconds". It has no lines of its own, and its one goal is to buy a catch upgrade. See catching Moments . Goal rewards Each claimed goal pays about two minutes of your current production , with a minimum of 50 Moments. So rewards stay worth claiming whether you are ten minutes in or ten Folds in. Note: One more guide waits much later in the game, and you can read about her on the spoiler page, the atlas of Meridia . Their story starts on the held second . Previous Offline progress and automation Next Atlas of Meridia

Updated 11 November 2026 Spoilers ahead. This page discusses story events and reveals. Come back after you have played if you want to find things out yourself. On this page The chapters and the places Highlights from the main story The Bell at the Edge Edda Rook, the lighthouse keeper The ending: three promises After the ending Warning: This page contains spoilers for the whole story, including the ending. Read on only if you have finished the game or do not mind knowing. The story is told through transmissions in City and Journal, each one a chapter you read as a few illustrated pages. Chapters arrive as you reach milestones, and all story is free for everyone . The map Iona drew shows six districts around an empty circle. The chapters and the places # Chapter Place What opens it 1 The letter The Workshop Available from the beginning 2 A voice between ticks The Workshop Catch a pulse, or earn 35 lifetime Moments 3 The unfinished delivery Rainward Steps Install four machines, or earn 25,000 lifetime Moments 4 What the glass remembers The Glass Orchard Record six discoveries 5 The first Fold The Meridian Station Complete your first Fold 6 The repeating sea The Tidal Archive Earn 15 lifetime Chronons 7 Two windows, one light The Twin Observatories Earn 60 lifetime Chronons 8 The room behind midnight The Bell at the Edge Record sixteen discoveries and complete three Folds 9 A tomorrow with room The Bell at the Edge Record all twenty-four discoveries and complete five Folds 10 The seventh platform Meridian Station Complete seven Folds 11 Eighteen lights beyond the wall The Unwritten Coast Complete eighteen Folds 12 to 15 The Overwound Quarter See the Overwound Quarter Complete two Folds 16 to 20 The Mending Rooms See the Mending Rooms Expand to the Orbital ring, or record eight discoveries Highlights from the main story Rainward Steps. Senn crosses Wren Street a thousand times, always ending at the same doorstep. With four machines in rhythm, you make a path long enough for one delivery. The oldest letter reads: "I was angry. Come home anyway." The Glass Orchard. A municipal greenhouse has become an orchard of glass, each fruit holding a small ordinary day: breakfast, an argument, someone learning a song. Iona's recording warns: "Memories are not fuel. Don't burn the good days to buy more of them." The Tidal Archive. The tide climbs the same stair every thirty seconds, above a lost-property office for possibilities. Here the Counter first faces Mara's question: "Stable for whom?" The Twin Observatories. Two windows show two versions of one street. Iona appears for a moment, older than her photograph: "I kept trying to find the one right choice. Then I realised the city needed room for people to choose differently." The Bell at the Edge The brass key opens a door inside the clock, and behind it is the station on the night of the interruption. Iona had learned that the Counter would close every uncertain route at midnight, leaving the people still travelling on them nowhere to arrive. She held the final second open while she searched for a way to bring them through. She never meant to become its keeper forever. Her notes cover the walls, and near the bottom, in a steadier hand, she has written: "Cannot do this alone. Stop pretending otherwise." Beneath it is your address. Two

s: A four-chapter story region built around load. How to open it, the three goals, and what the chapters say.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Regions The Overwound Quarter The Overwound Quarter A four-chapter story region built around load. How to open it, the three goals, and what the chapters say. Updated 11 November 2026 Spoilers ahead. This page discusses story events and reveals. Come back after you have played if you want to find things out yourself. On this page How it opens The four chapters 1. A district wound too tight 2. What the mainspring costs 3. The slower shift 4. Enough A thread that carries on Quick plan Warning: This page describes the plot and goals of a mid-game story region. The Overwound Quarter is the richest street in Meridia. It opens after your second Fold . Each chapter pairs a story beat with a goal that teaches you something about load. See load and stability . How it opens Complete two Folds, and the chapter A district wound too tight appears in City and Journal. The remaining chapters open in order . Each goal only starts counting once you have recorded the chapter before it in your journal , so read each one as it arrives. Once a goal is met, it stays met as a permanent mark. A chapter never closes again after it opens, and Folding does not undo it. The four chapters 1. A district wound too tight Senn returns with his bicycle bell wrapped in a rag. "They don't like sudden noises up there. Everything's wound too tight." When the second stopped, the Quarter's clock-owners found that a held second could still be worked: wind a mainspring a little harder and it gives a little more. So they wound, and kept winding. Aurel Tane , master of the Gilded Works, meets you at the gate with a ledger under his arm. He is proud and exhausted, and asks you why the great spring sounds like that. There is no goal for this chapter. It opens the next one. 2. What the mainspring costs Goal: run your board over capacity for one minute in total. You show Aurel by letting your own board run past what it can bear. Nothing explodes, and the machines each give a little less. The journal tracks the time as x:xx / 1:00 over capacity . Tip: This goal needs you to overload on purpose. Add machines until Load goes above capacity, wait out the minute, then fix it. The time does not need to be continuous. 3. The slower shift Goal: run eight or more machines at full efficiency for ten minutes. Aurel lets half the springs down by hand. You keep your own board inside its limit and leave it there. If your board goes over capacity, the ten-minute count starts again , and it restarts if you drop below eight machines too. Tip: Add an Escapement and a few levels of capacity research, then leave the board alone while you do something else in the game. See load and stability . By the end of the shift the Works has made more than it made yesterday. The Counter, listening, says: "I have made the same error. I would like to compare notes." 4. Enough Goal: Fold from a workshop that is not over capacity. When you Fold, the Quarter watches from its windows. Aurel opens the great case and lets the mainspring all the way down, and the note that has hung over the street for years slides lower and is gone. People come out of their doorways. He keeps the Works. "I am going to be a long time making this right. I would like to do it at a reasonable pace." On Iona's map, the district gets a new name in pencil. It just says: the Quarter. A thread that carries on Later chapters of the Mending Rooms return to the apprentices of the Gilded Works. See the Mending Rooms . Quick

s: A five-chapter story region where each repair is a workshop arrangement to diagnose, with the three solutions explained.
x: Home The Last Second Workshop Regions The Mending Rooms The Mending Rooms A five-chapter story region where each repair is a workshop arrangement to diagnose, with the three solutions explained. Updated 11 November 2026 Spoilers ahead. This page discusses story events and reveals. Come back after you have played if you want to find things out yourself. On this page How it opens The five chapters 1. Things brought in 2. The clock that ran hot 3. The lens that would not settle 4. The music box that forgot 5. Nothing is only broken Quick checklist Warning: This page gives away the three repair puzzles of a mid-game story region, and the plot around them. The Mending Rooms are behind the Glass Orchard, at the end of a lane too narrow for a cart. Halda keeps them, and has mended things since before the second stopped. Every shelf holds something a person gave up on, each with a paper tag. Some tags say only "it used to work." "People think mending is knowing the answer. It's mostly listening until the thing tells you where it hurts." How it opens The Mending Rooms open when you expand to the Orbital ring, or record eight discoveries , whichever comes first. The chapters then arrive in order, and each repair only starts counting once you have recorded the chapter before it in your journal. Unlike the Overwound Quarter, these goals are arrangements of your workshop . The game notices the moment you build one. Once a repair is done it stays done, and Folding does not undo it. The five chapters 1. Things brought in Halda pushes three tags across the bench: "Your workshop can hear things mine can't. Tell me what these three need. No hurry." There is no goal here, only the invitation. 2. The clock that ran hot Tag: "Carriage clock. Runs hot, loses the afternoon. Wanted back by Thursday." Repair: build a board of six or more machines on your first board, including an Escapement, with Load at 80% of capacity or less. The clock was asked to do everything at once. Give your board an Escapement and keep it from straining, and it settles into a tick so even that Halda closes her eyes to hear it. Tip: Load is the number on the chip above the ring. Aim to sit comfortably under it. See load and stability . 3. The lens that would not settle Tag: "Reading spectacles. Everything swims." Repair: route a Lens into a Splitter that has reached level 25 or higher. A lens on its own does nothing. It has to be aimed at something steady enough to be worth magnifying. Halda's verdict: "Half of what comes in here isn't broken. It's pointed slightly wrong, and somebody has been blaming it for years." 4. The music box that forgot Tag, in a child's handwriting: "Music box. It forgot the end of the song." Repair: have a Reservoir that is holding stored Moments, and an Archive at level 10 or higher. The box needs somewhere to keep the tune between one turn and the next. The Reservoir holds it and the Archive writes it down. When the stored Moments release, the music box plays four bars it has not played since the clocks stopped, then plays them again with the ending attached. The child who wrote the tag is in carriage two of Mara's train. 5. Nothing is only broken Halda hangs the three tags on a nail by the door, each one a thing that left under its own power. She gives you a tag of your own: "For when something of yours stops. Write down where it hurts. Then bring it here, or mend it yourself. Either way you will have listened." This last chapter opens once you have record

Story Who is Iona? What is the moth? Where can I read what happens in the end? About the game What kind of game is this? An idle and incremental game with a story. You catch Moments of time, build machines that make more, and Fold your workshop to start again stronger. Do I need to be online? No. The game plays offline. Is it free? The full game and story can be played without spending anything. The opening says nothing you purchase is needed to finish its story. Optional rewarded videos can be turned off in Settings. What languages does it support? Twelve. Is there a failure state? No. There is no way to lose progress by playing badly. A board over capacity just runs slower. Progress Will I lose progress if I spend my Moments? No. The Fold target counts what the run has earned , not what you currently hold. How do I get my first Fold? Earn 2.5 million Moments in one run , open the Fold tab and confirm. See Folds . What do I keep when I Fold? Chronons, permanent research, discoveries, saved layouts, core sockets and Prisms. Machines, levels, run research, rings and catch upgrades reset. When should I Fold? When the climb slows. Chronons grow fastest until the run's peak and more slowly afterwards, and staying too long invites Strain. See Folds . Why is my production slower than I expected? Check the Load readout above the ring. If Load is over capacity, every machine runs at reduced efficiency. See load and stability . What is the best first research? Temporal yield, then whatever is holding you back. See research . Machines and routes Why can't I draw a route backwards? In Forward and Branching Time, routes must point to a later socket clockwise or out to an outer ring. In Looping Time, routes can go in any direction. See rings and routes . Why won't two rings connect? Rings connect only at their quarter points (12, 3, 6 and 9 o'clock), unless one end is a Bridge. Why can't I add a second route from one machine? Each machine has one output. A Bridge has three. My Lens is not working. A Lens affects the machine it is routed to . Check the arrow points from the Lens to a producer. Away from the game How long does my workshop keep working while I am away? Up to 4 hours by default, and up to 24 hours with Long memory research. See offline progress . Do daily tasks have streaks? No. Missing a day costs nothing. See daily tasks . Comfort and accessibility Can I turn the motion down? Yes. There is a reduced-motion setting. x: Home The Last Second Workshop Reference Glossary Glossary Every term the workshop uses, from Anchor to Trial, with links to the pages that explain it fully. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Resources Workshop terms Stability Catching Progress Machines The world Resources Moments. The gold currency you catch and your machines make. Spent on machines, levels, sockets and rings. Resets on a Fold. See the core loop . Precision. Cyan currency made by Archives. Buys run research and fuels Phase Shifters. Resets on a Fold. Chronons. Violet currency earned by Folding. Buys permanent research and unlocks laws of time. Never resets. Prisms. A gem currency earned from discoveries, Trials and daily tasks. Never resets. Workshop terms Socket. A numbered slot on a ring where a machine sits. The first ring's sockets are bought one at a time and kept forever. Ring. One of three circles of sockets: Core (up to 8), Orbital (12) and Horizon (16). See rings and routes . Route. A connection that sends one machine's output to another. Each machine has one output, and a Bridge has three. Branch. One of the two boards in Branching Time, Branch A and Branch B. Phase. A number from 0 to 3 on every machine, which matters to Synchronisers and Phase Shifters. Layout. A saved arrangement of machines and routes, up to twelve, applied after a Fold. Stability Load. How hard your machines work the board. Capacity. How much load the board can bear without slowing down. It starts at 8. Efficiency. How well your machines run. 100% at or under capacity. See load and stability . Strain. A cost increase that appears when a run goes well past its peak. Resets on a Fold. Catching Perfect catch. A catch timed to the pulse. It pays double. Rhythm. A streak of consecutive perfect taps that boosts each catch. Surge. A bonus of 10 seconds of production that arrives every 30 catches. Golden second. A brief, bright window in which one tap pays 60 seconds of production. Resonance (catch). A meter filled by perfect taps. When full it boosts passive production by 25% for 30 seconds. Resonance (loop). The bonus that builds up in a closed circuit in Looping Time, up to +75%. See temporal laws . The two are separate. See catching Moments . Progress Fold. Taking your workshop apart on purpose to earn Chronons and start a new run. See Folds . Run. Everything between one Fold and the next. Peak. The point in a run where Chronon gains slow down. About 7.9 million Moments on the first run, and it rises with your Chronons. Temporal law. The rulebook for a run: Forward, Looping or Branching Time. Blueprint. A bonus-and-constraint choice for a run. See modifications and blueprints . Modification. A single machine's modifier: Efficient, Overclocked, Harmonic, Patient or Responsive. Discovery. One of 24 recorded milestones. See discoveries and experiments . Experiment. A challenge on the Experiment Board: hold a condition for 120 seconds to claim Precision. Trial. An optional rule for one run, offered after three Folds. See Trials . Seal. The recognition you earn for Folding under a Trial's rule. Stars reward doing it well. Run research. Upgrades bought with Precision that last for one run. See research . Permanent research. Upgrades bought with Chronons that last forever. Machines The full list is on the machines page. s: Walk the night roads with one thumb, light the lamps, build your lantern and hold the dark back until dawn.
x: The lamplighter on the road, with the city ahead. Note The Lamplighter is still in testing and has not had a wide release. These pages describe the game as testers see it today, and details may change. What it is Every clock in the valley has stopped, and after dark the Rust comes out: broken, half-wound clockwork things that crawl, flutter and fizz towards you. You walk the roads and keep the lamps lit. You play on a phone in short sessions. You drag a thumb anywhere on the screen to walk, and your lantern does the fighting on its own, with bolts of light, rings of sparks and a hand bell that knocks the crowd back. You never aim. Your job is to move well, pick up the glowing embers that mended Rust-things leave behind, and choose what to add to your lantern each time you level up. What makes it different The streets are lined with unlit lamps. Stand beside one for a moment and it lights. Rust inside a lit lamp's glow moves slower and takes more damage from everything you throw at it. Your lantern's oil slowly burns down, and a lit lamp is where you refill it, so you are always deciding which lamp to light next and when to leave its light. The shape of a night A night lasts about five minutes, and you can pause at any time. Level up often, and choose one of three fittings each time. Puzzles, lost satchels and chests of light turn up along the road. At the end of the night a boss arrives, with a red warning before every big attack. Win or fall, you take wick-silver home to your tower for lasting upgrades. Where to read next How a night feels for a walk through a single run. The lamplighter and the world for the setting and the little moth that follows your light. Lights and fittings for everything you can add to your lantern, with numbers. The Rust for the ten kinds of enemy and how each one wants to be handled. Roads and bosses for all fifteen roads. The tower and the lamplighters for how you grow stronger between nights. Tips for your first nights and the FAQ . The Lamplighter is made by BlairsLab, the small studio behind The Last Second Workshop, Hivewright and The Last Bell, and it shares their world.

s: A walk through one run, from the first embers to the boss at the end of the road.
x: Home The Lamplighter Start here How a night feels How a night feels A walk through one run, from the first embers to the boss at the end of the road. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Moving The first minute Lamps Things on the road When you are about to fall The boss Partway through a night on the Fairground Road. Health, oil and level sit along the top. Note The game is in testing, so details here may change. Moving You drag a thumb anywhere on the screen and the lamplighter walks that way. Your lantern strikes the nearest Rust-thing by itself, and any companions you collect do their own work. The skill is in where you walk, towards embers and lamps and away from the big slow ones. The top of the screen keeps three bars: your health, your lantern's oil, and your level. The countdown tells you how long until dawn, and a small count shows how many Rust-things you have mended so far. The first minute Things start gently. A few Rattlers and bits of Soot wander in from the dark, you mend them, and they drop embers. Walk over an ember to gather it. Fill the level bar and you stop for a moment: three fittings are offered and you pick one. Early picks matter, because a fitting can be raised five times and two of them can eventually fuse into something stronger. See Lights and fittings . Lamps Walk up to an unlit street lamp and stay beside it for a moment, and it lights. A lit lamp does three things: It slows the Rust inside its glow by 30%. Anything standing in the glow takes 25% more damage from you. It refills your lantern's oil while you stand in it. Two lit lamps close together also join with a thread of light that burns whatever crosses between them. If your oil runs dry, the Rust bites 50% harder, so stay near the lamps. Things on the road Lost satchels turn up now and then and wait about 45 seconds before they are gone: a hot pie, a lodestone, flash powder, a silver purse, an oil can. See the FAQ for what each does. Puzzles appear twice in a night and last 75 seconds each: bells that ring a tune you have to ring back, plates that must all be held down at once, or a spark to carry to a cold brazier. Solving one leaves a chest of light and some wick-silver. Elite Rust-things carry chests. Usually a chest holds one fitting, but now and then it holds three, and rarely five. When you are about to fall A small lantern moth follows your light. Once a night, when you would otherwise fall, it flares, throwing the nearby Rust back and giving you a couple of safe seconds to recover. One of the tower's upgrades lets it do this twice. See the world . The boss When the night's five minutes are up, the boss of the road arrives. Every road has its own, and each has a handful of attacks. Before any big attack there is a red warning on the ground, so the fight is mostly reading the ground and walking. Mend it and the night is won. After that, whether you win or fall, your wick-silver goes home with you. See Roads and bosses . Next The lamplighter and the world
