Updated 11 November 2026 On this page A world that stopped The lamplighters The lantern moth The roads The title screen: the road, the lamp, and the city in the rain. Note The game is in testing, so details may change. A world that stopped Every clock in the valley has stopped. On the roads between the valley and a city that stands still in the rain, the Rust comes out after dark. These are broken, half-wound clockwork things from fairgrounds, mills, markets and railway cuttings. The lamps along those roads have to be lit again every night. The Lamplighter shares a world with the other BlairsLab games. You do not need any of them to play this one. The lamplighters You begin as Linnet , keeper of the Wayward Light and the first to walk the road. Other lamplighters can be earned by playing, each with a different first fitting and a small strength: a tinker, a bell-ringer, a quick runner, a lock-keeper from the canal, and a clockmaker from the city who came out to see why the lamps went dark. Their names and how to open them are on The tower and the lamplighters . Linnet, the first lamplighter. The lantern moth A small moth follows your light along every road. Once a night, when you are about to fall, it flares. The nearby Rust is thrown back, you are safe for two seconds, and you get back up with some of your health restored. A tower upgrade called The moth stays lets it save you twice a night. The lantern moth. The roads Fifteen roads run from the fairground at the valley's edge, through orchards, a stopped weir, a market and a canal, over a long bridge hung with silent bells, and on to the city gate and the wall beyond. Each has its own scenery, its own weather in the air (confetti, leaves, mist, sparks, wind, rain hanging still, embers), its own lamps and its own boss. They are listed on Roads and bosses . Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Reference The four with habits Which roads have what Handling a crowd The Rust, left to right and top to bottom: Rattler, Soot, Shieldback, Crow, Rustling, Brute, Oil-spitter, Tick-bomb, Douser, Cog-heap. Note The game is in testing. These are today's numbers and they may change. The Rust is what is left of the old fairgrounds, mills and markets: broken, half-wound things that come at you in waves. Mend one and it drops embers to gather. The first six are simple. The last four each have a habit, and the game shows a short note the first time each one turns up. Reference Health, speed and damage are the starting values on a first night. Speed is in tiles a second (you walk at 3.6). Rust-things grow tougher the further along the roads you go and on harder nights, so treat these as the baseline. Rust-thing Health Speed Bite Embers Notes Rattler 9 1.55 9 1 The everyday walker. Soot 5 2.5 6 1 Fragile and fast. Shieldback 38 1.1 14 3 Armoured and slow. Crow 8 3.0 7 2 Flies, so scenery does not stop it. Rustling 18 1.85 11 2 A sturdier Rattler. Brute 140 0.9 24 10 Huge and slow, and worth a lot of embers. Oil-spitter 14 1.5 8 2 Keeps its distance and spits oil. Tick-bomb 10 2.2 6 2 Runs at you and goes off. Douser 24 1.6 8 3 Puts out lit lamps. Cog-heap 32 1.2 12 1 Falls apart into three Rattlers. The four with habits Oil-spitter. It stays about five tiles away and spits oil at you. Running away only makes it follow at range, so walk at it. Tick-bomb. It runs in, fizzes for just under a second, and goes off in a ring a little over two tiles wide. The blast hurts other Rust as well. Step out of the ring, or mend it before it arrives. Douser. It heads for the nearest lit lamp and puts it out. Stop it, then light the lamp again. A snuffed lamp gives off a puff of smoke. Cog-heap. When you mend it, it falls apart into three Rattlers, so make sure you have room to deal with them. Which roads have what Different roads send different mixes of Rust. The first road, the Fairground Road, uses only Rattlers, Soot, Shieldbacks and Brutes. The four habit-having kinds start arriving from Orchard Lane onwards. The full rosters are on Roads and bosses . Handling a crowd Keep moving, and use lit lamps as your slow-down zones: Rust in the light moves 30% slower and takes 25% more damage. Save your good positions for Brutes. They are slow, and circling one while your fittings work is the safest way to mend it. Do not stand still near Dousers and Tick-bombs. More in Tips for your first nights . This page names every boss, so skip it if you would rather meet them in the dark. How roads and nights work There are fifteen roads. Each ends in a boss that arrives once the night's five minutes are up. Every road has three nights: Night I is the first visit. Winning it opens the next road. Night II opens after you win Night I, and Night III after Night II. They bring more Rust, tougher Rust and harder-hitting Rust, and the boss's attacks get fiercer. Each road is harder than the one before it. Every boss has a set of attacks, and each big attack has a red warning on the ground first. s: Practical habits for lighting lamps, choosing fittings and getting the first boss down.
x: Home The Lamplighter Guides Tips for your first nights Tips for your first nights Practical habits for lighting lamps, choosing fittings and getting the first boss down. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page On the road Building your lantern Bosses Between nights Note The game is in testing, so details here may change. On the road Light the lamps early. Each one takes only a moment of standing beside it, and every lit lamp slows the Rust in its glow by 30% and makes them take 25% more damage. The first road has eight. Watch your oil. When the lantern runs dry the Rust bites 50% harder. A lit lamp refills it as long as you stand in its glow, so work your route from lamp to lamp. Use the lines. Two lit lamps within about ten tiles of each other are joined by a thread of light that burns what crosses it. If you can lead a crowd across one, you get free damage. Keep moving. Your lantern aims itself, so never stop to shoot. Grab the satchels. They vanish after about 45 seconds. A lodestone pulls every ember on the road to you, and a hot pie mends a third of your health. Building your lantern Chase a fusion. Taking one weapon to level 5 and holding its partner fitting turns it into something much stronger. Lantern beam with Sharp lenses, Hand bell with Wider light and Tin hound with Thick coat are all natural pairs. See Lights and fittings . Do not spread thin. You can carry five weapons, but a few well-raised ones beat many level-ones. Passives help everything. Sharp lenses, Wider light and Winding key improve every weapon you have. Reroll, banish or skip. If three choices are all wrong for you, take the silver for skipping. Banishing a fitting you will never want makes better ones turn up more often. Open the chests. Elite chests give free picks, and a solved puzzle's chest always holds three. Bosses Read the red. Every big attack warns you on the ground first. Move out of the red and return to attack. Fight near light. Lit lamps near the boss's arena make it take 25% more damage while it stands in their glow. Rain, Snuff and Spiral each need a different answer: step off the marked ground, relight lamps when Snuff puts them out, and slip between the arms of a Spiral. Come back stronger. If a boss beats you, spend your silver in the tower and try again. Between nights Put early silver into Sturdier keeper , Bigger tank and Keen edge : cheap, and they help every night. Try your new lamplighters. Odo, Ismay, Corrie and Ambrose open after Night I of particular roads, and Tuck after any Night II. See The tower and the lamplighters . If a road is too hard, a different lamplighter or a few polishes on your lantern parts can be enough. Previous From the same world Next Frequently asked questions

s: An endless wall-defence loot shooter where you hold the wall of Belcourt against waves of clockwork Rust, aiming with one thumb.
x: Dusk over Belcourt, with the gunner on the wall. Note The Belfry Gun is in closed testing and is not widely released yet. This section covers what is in the game today, and details, numbers and features may change. The one-line pitch You are the last gunner on the wall of Belcourt, the little town under the great clocktower. The Rust, a swarm of clockwork creatures, comes up the hill in endless waves. You aim with your thumb, hold to fire, and keep the wall standing as long as you can. Every run starts from nothing but a plain gun and a bare wall. Why it is fun One thumb. Touch and hold anywhere on the field and the gunner aims at your thumb and fires. Lift to stop. Every gun is different. Loot drops from the Rust in seven rarities, each with its own rolled traits, so no two runs play the same. Endless, and brutal. The Rust grows tougher faster than your loot does. Losing is the normal ending. A town in the middle of the fight. Every five waves you make camp in Belcourt: feed the hens, eat at the inn, pray at the chapel, shop the market, patch the wall. Something lasts. Your gun and loot vanish when the wall falls, but medals feed the Belfry's Memory, and milestones unlock new skills, loot and characters. A very long goal. Wave 200 is the long-term target. x: Home The Belfry Gun Start here A Run, Start to Finish A Run, Start to Finish A single run of The Belfry Gun, from picking a gun to the wall falling. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page 1. Choose a plain gun 2. Hold the wall 3. Level up as you shoot 4. Every fifth wave, make camp 5. Every tenth wave, a boss 6. The moth 7. The wall falls Note The game is in closed testing, so what you read here describes the game as testers see it today. Every run in The Belfry Gun ends with the wall falling. What counts is how far you got and what you did with the loot and brass on the way. Holding the wall mid-run. The wave counter is at the top. 1. Choose a plain gun You begin with a choice of four starting guns: a pistol, a rifle, a scattergun or a big gun. They are deliberately plain. You pick your character as well, and each one has a favourite gun and a quirk (see Unlocks and characters ). 2. Hold the wall Waves arrive one after another. Each is bigger and tougher than the last: the Rust gets about 11% tougher every wave, and it hits the wall about 8.5% harder. A wave starts at 10 Rust and grows until it is 36 strong (not counting swarm clumps or boss escorts). Breaks between waves are short, at 1.5 seconds. There is a "bring the next wave now" button, which pays bonus brass for not waiting. 3. Level up as you shoot Kills give XP. Each level, the game offers three skills and you pick one, for this run only. Weapon skills only appear for the kind of gun you are carrying. Details live in Skills and the workshop . 4. Every fifth wave, make camp After wave 5, 10, 15 and so on, the gunner makes camp in Belcourt and nothing moves until you leave. You wear the loot you found, break down what you do not want for brass, spend that brass at the workshop, and visit the town. See Belcourt, between waves . 5. Every tenth wave, a boss The fight changes place every ten waves, and the tenth wave of each place brings a boss. Bosses have habits: some split, some charge, some summon, some wear heavy plate. More in The Rust . 6. The moth Once per run, when the wall is nearly gone (15% or less), the lantern moth settles on the stones and mends 30% of it. Some characters and some lucky charms bring the moth back for a second visit. The lantern moth: one mend per run, unless a character or charm brings it back. 7. The wall falls When it does, you get one revive per run, which brings the wall back at half strength. After that, your records are counted, your medals are paid out, and a new run begins. The run is saved at every camp, so closing the app never costs you more than a few waves. Tip Medals from every run go into the Belfry's Memory, so even a short run makes the next one a little stronger. See The Belfry's Memory . Next FAQ

s: How the thumb controls work, how the four starting guns differ, and what the wall does for you.
x: Home The Belfry Gun Guides The Gun and the Wall The Gun and the Wall How the thumb controls work, how the four starting guns differ, and what the wall does for you. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Controls: one thumb The wall The four starting guns Which one should you start with? Note The Belfry Gun is in closed testing. Numbers here are what the game uses today and may change. Controls: one thumb Touch and hold anywhere on the field. The gunner aims at your thumb and fires as fast as the gun allows. Lift your thumb to stop firing. The gun reloads by itself when it runs empty, or after a moment of not firing. There are no buttons to hunt for mid-fight, so your other hand is free. The wall The wall runs across the bottom of the field, and the gunner stands on top of it. Rust that reaches the stones chews on them, and the wall is your health bar: when it falls, the run ends. Spitters and Gargoyles can hurt it from range, so killing what is near is not always enough. The wall stones. Plenty of things help the wall: coats, wall stones and plating at the workshop, the chapel, the mortar crew, the lantern moth, and the Belfry's Memory between runs. Do not put everything into damage, because a big gun is no use if the wall is gone. The four starting guns Every run begins with one of four plain guns. Here are their base numbers before any loot, skills or character perks. Gun Damage Shots a second Magazine Reload (s) Crit Special Pistol 10 4.0 10 1.0 8% Fast, light, quick reload, good at crits Rifle 32 1.25 5 1.6 5% Slow and hard-hitting; shots pierce Scattergun 9 per pellet 1.6 5 1.4 5% Five pellets in a cone; knocks the Rust back Big gun 36 0.9 3 1.8 4% A slow mortar that bursts where it lands The pistol: quick and light. Which one should you start with? Pistol. The friendliest. It fires quickly and is forgiving when you are still learning where to aim. Rifle. Slow, but each hit counts, and it pierces. Great against armoured Rust, where small hits are mostly wasted. Scattergun. Good against crowds and swarms, because pellets spread and knock things back. Big gun. Slow bursts that hit whole groups where they land. Rewarding if you lead your shots. The big gun, a slow hand mortar. Tip A gun's own skills only work while you carry that kind of gun. If you swap to a different class mid-run, those picks stop helping. See Skills and the workshop . Loot can replace your gun during a run. See Guns and loot . The market Restock it for three pieces of gear, a level better than what drops, bought with brass. Searching Go looking in the dark streets. You might find brass, loot, a stray hen, a lesson (a free skill pick), or nothing. The hen house Buy hens with brass, each a little dearer than the last. Hens lay eggs worth brass at every visit. Several of these cost hours (supper and prayer take an hour each), so you cannot do everything every visit. The pack The Pack tab shows the gear you have found. For each piece, the game shows how wearing it would change your damage and the wall. You can: Wear it. Break it down into brass. Better rarities pay far more (see Guns and loot ). Your pack holds 24 pieces. If it fills, the game breaks down the weakest piece automatically so you never miss a drop. The workshop The Workshop tab is where brass becomes wall stones, plating, a mortar crew, a second gunner and more. Full list in Skills and the workshop . Settling in The run is saved at every camp. There is a "bring the next wave now" button between waves for the impatient. The Belfry's Memory can start later runs partway up the hill. See The Belfry's Memory . Tip Hens pay back slowly, so they are best bought early. A hen bought on your first visit lays eggs on every later visit. Previous The Gun and the Wall Next Tips for Deeper Waves

s: Every kind of clockwork foe, the elite twists, the twelve places on the hill and the bosses that guard them.
x: Home The Belfry Gun Reference The Rust The Rust Every kind of clockwork foe, the elite twists, the twelve places on the hill and the bosses that guard them. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The kinds Elites Twelve places, round and round Four boss habits Note The Belfry Gun is in closed testing. Foe numbers are today's and may change. The kinds The health below is for wave 1. It grows by about 11% every wave. Kind Health Habit Crawler 20 Plain walker. The bulk of every wave. Skitter 10 Small and quick, zig-zagging up the hill. Moth-eater 14 Flies, and weaves from side to side. Plated 60 Slow and armoured: every hit loses 6 damage. Big single hits get through. Spitter 24 Stops halfway and spits rust at the wall from range. Swarmling 6 Arrives in clumps of six. Scatterguns and big guns sweep them up. Roller 34 A plated wheel that rolls straight at the wall, fast. (Clockmakers' Quarter onward.) Gargoyle 30 Flies down from the rooftops, weaves, and spits from high up the hill. (High Wall only.) A Plated: small hits barely hurt it. Tip Armour takes a flat amount off every hit, so ten tiny hits are worse than one big one. Rifles and big guns do well against Plated Rust. Elites From wave 12, some Rust turn up elite . The chance climbs with depth, and by deep waves up to about a third of a wave can be elite. Elites have 1.5 times the health, but pay triple brass, double XP and drop loot far more often. There are four kinds, and they open up as you go deeper. Elite Twist Shielded A shield soaks up its first hits. Swift It moves much faster. Splitting It splits in two when it falls. Mending It mends the Rust around it. Twelve places, round and round Every ten waves the fight moves to a new place in town, each with its own mix of Rust and its own boss. There are twelve places in three districts. After the twelfth, the hill starts over, with much tougher Rust. Every boss beaten also pays a medal toward the Belfry's Memory. An armoured boss. Hit it hard, not often. Four boss habits Every boss uses one of four tricks: Split. Kill it and it becomes two. Keep your fire up. Charge. It stalls, then lunges. Save your best shots for the lunge. Summon. It calls Skitters. Clear the escort or the wall pays for it. Armour. A thick plate, so big single hits and armour-ignoring skills work best. See also Tips for deeper waves and Guns and loot .

Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Earning medals The upgrades Marching orders Keystones Note The Belfry Gun is in closed testing. Costs, caps and keystones are today's and may change. Your gun, loot and brass never survive a run. The Belfry's Memory is a small set of deep, permanent upgrades bought with medals . With enough runs, a player who loses at wave 25 today can reach wave 200. The Memory screen: keystones up top, upgrades below. Earning medals Every run pays medals for the waves it cleared: A fifth of a medal per wave , plus a little extra for depth (deeper waves pay more). One medal for every boss beaten. Medals are rounded down at the end of the run. A run that clears 30 waves and three bosses pays about 10 medals. A boss is worth much more than an ordinary wave, so reaching the tenth wave of a place pays. The upgrades Each level costs a little more than the last (the first level costs the base amount, and each further level adds the step). Values below are medals. s: Practical habits that add waves, from reading the Rust to spending brass at camp.
x: Home The Belfry Gun Guides Tips for Deeper Waves Tips for Deeper Waves Practical habits that add waves, from reading the Rust to spending brass at camp. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Reading the field Spending well Picking skills Between runs Note The Belfry Gun is in closed testing. Tips are based on how the game works today and may need adjusting as it changes. The Rust grows about 11% tougher every wave and your wall takes about 8.5% more damage. Nothing you carry keeps up forever, so these tips push the end later. Reading the field Match your gun to the foe. Scatterguns and big guns sweep Swarmlings. Rifles punch through Plated armour. Pistols mop up the small and quick. Kill what shoots first. Spitters and Gargoyles damage the wall from range, so they are often the priority even when something bigger is closer. Learn the boss habits (split, charge, summon, armour). Each has a clear answer, covered in The Rust . Lead your shots with the big gun. Its burst lands where you aim, so aim ahead of moving targets. Spending well Spend brass at every camp. Unspent brass is lost when the wall falls, so put it into the wall and your damage. Balance the wall and the gun. Wall stones and plating buy time; damage upgrades end waves sooner. See Skills and the workshop . Buy hens early. They lay eggs every visit, so a hen bought sooner pays more times. See Belcourt, between waves . Use the town hours wisely. You get three per visit. Supper (+50% XP for five waves) helps when you want skills, and prayer (the wall takes 20% less for five waves) helps before a boss. Compare gear properly. The Pack screen shows what each piece does to your damage and the wall. Trust that over the rarity colour. Picking skills Gun-specific skills only work for the gun you carry. If you plan to swap guns, think before you pick. When the list runs out, veteran perks fill in. They are small but permanent for the run, so even late levels help. Take a wall skill when the wall is hurting. Extra Stones and Thick Skin are good picks. Between runs Spend medals every time. Even a short run pays a few, and the Belfry's Memory compounds. See The Belfry's Memory . Chase the milestones. Heavy Rounds at wave 8, burning loot at wave 11 and the second gunner at wave 15 are all worth working towards. See Unlocks and characters . Try other characters. Some bring a second moth, a free helper or a stronger wall. A Plated: one big hit works better than many small ones. Tip The moth only mends once per run (some characters and one named charm bring it back again). Warning Closing the app mid-wave only loses what happened since your last camp, so stop after a camp if you can. Previous Belcourt, Between Waves Next Guns and Loot

s: Quick answers about the closed test, runs, loot, the Memory, characters and wave 200.
x: Home The Belfry Gun Start here FAQ FAQ Quick answers about the closed test, runs, loot, the Memory, characters and wave 200. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Is it out yet? How do I play? Does it ever end? Why is it so hard? What carries over between runs? Is there an actual wave 200? What does the moth do? Can I stop mid-run? Which gun should I start with? What are the loot rarities? Do I need to know the other BlairsLab games? Note The Belfry Gun is in closed testing. Anything here may change. Is it out yet? Not widely. It is in closed testing for now. How do I play? Touch and hold anywhere on the field. The gunner aims at your thumb and fires. Lift to stop. See The gun and the wall . Does it ever end? The waves do not, but every run ends when the wall falls and you start again. Why is it so hard? On purpose. The Rust grows tougher faster than your loot does. A new player should expect to fall somewhere around wave 20 to 40 at first. What carries over between runs? Only records, unlocks and the Belfry's Memory. Your gun, loot, brass, skills and workshop upgrades all start from nothing. See Unlocks and characters and The Belfry's Memory . Is there an actual wave 200? Waves are endless, so yes, and beyond. It is a long-term goal, and the Belfry's Memory is deep enough to get players there eventually. Reaching it with a character also opens that character's partner. What does the moth do? Once per run, when the wall is down to 15% or less, the lantern moth mends 30% of it. Some characters and items bring it back more than once. The moth's favour can make it mend even more. Can I stop mid-run? Yes. The run is saved at every camp (every fifth wave), so closing the app never loses more than a few waves. Which gun should I start with? Pistol is the friendliest, the rifle rewards patience, the scattergun suits crowds and the big gun suits players who lead their shots. See The gun and the wall . What are the loot rarities? Common, Fine, Rare, Heirloom, Masterwork, Relic and Legendary. The last three open as you reach waves 30, 60 and 100. See Guns and loot . Do I need to know the other BlairsLab games? No. Belcourt shares a world with them, and a few faces from The Last Second Workshop pass through, but nothing carries between games. Previous A Run, Start to Finish Next The Gun and the Wall

s: A story RPG about winding the world's stopped clocks back up, one town at a time, with a courier, a clockmaker and a small moth made of light.
x: Wicklow Halt, where the story begins, and a station clock that has never once been late. Note The Roads Between is in closed testing and has not had a wide release. Everything on these pages describes the game as it stands today and may change before release, including numbers, names and what is in each chapter. What it is The Roads Between is a story RPG of about thirty to forty hours, set in the same world as the other BlairsLab games. The great clocks of the Evenwold have stopped, the small towns have gone still, and the Rust (clockwork creatures gone to rust) has moved in. Wren , a courier's apprentice who has never been further than the next town, sets out with a clockmaker who walked out of his guild and a small moth made of soft golden light. They wind the world back up one town at a time. Every chapter ends with a town's clock running again, the people you met frozen mid-step finishing what they were doing, and the colour coming back. There are two parts. Part One runs from Chapter 1 to Chapter 10. Part Two begins with Chapter 11, and Chapters 11 to 14 are playable today. How it plays You walk the world. Towns, roads and dungeons are maps you explore on foot. Doors take you between them, and a hidden chest or a sealed door is often the moth's cue. The Rust is visible. Rust wanders the maps and notices you from a few tiles away. Touching one starts a fight. There are no random battles, so you choose what to take on. See Exploring and saving . Battles are turn-based and readable. A turn-order bar shows who acts next, and you can bend it. You spend Wind on skills, fill a Chime for a limit move, and use Chains with friends you are close to. See Battle basics . Bosses are hard on purpose. Most players lose a boss fight the first time unless they have trained a little. A few extra battles beforehand make it a fair fight, and losing costs you nothing. See Training and difficulty . There is more than the road. You can craft, cook, fish, play a card game called Cogs , climb the ranks of the Arena , and track down optional hunts . Where to start If you want to... Read Know what the story is about, with no spoilers The world and the story Learn the first hour Getting started Be ready for the first boss Training and difficulty Understand fights Battle basics and Elements and statuses Meet the party The party Find your way through a region Chapters Look up a Rust, item or shop Bestiary , Weapons , Shops Check a word Glossary and FAQ and tips Spoilers Every page is spoiler-free unless its description says otherwise. Pages with spoilers are labelled, and each chapter has two pages: a region guide with no spoilers, and a separate plot and boss page that gives the story and the boss fight away. Late party members are kept on their own labelled pages too.

s: The setup of The Roads Between, with no spoilers - the Evenwold, the stopped clocks and the people who set out to wind them.
x: Home The Roads Between Start here The world and the story The world and the story The setup of The Roads Between, with no spoilers - the Evenwold, the stopped clocks and the people who set out to wind them. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The premise What to expect The two parts A shared world A moth made of soft light taps at Wren's window on the morning the clocks stop. The premise The Evenwold is a world of small towns joined by old roads. The towns' clocks have stopped, nobody has wound them, and the Rust has moved in. Wren is a courier's apprentice at the post office in Wicklow Halt. She has never been further than the next town. One morning the 6:12 to Tollbridge, which in forty years has never once been late, does not come at all. The whole village has stopped mid-step, her Aunt Agnes included, and a small moth made of soft light is tapping at her window. With a clockmaker who walked out of his guild, a lantern moth that will not leave her alone, and the friends she meets along the road, Wren sets out to wind the world back up. What to expect Light mood. The Rust is a problem to solve, not a horror, and a good many of the people you free from stopped time are very funny about it. A clock at the end of every chapter. Each chapter ends by mending a town's clock. The town wakes, colour comes back, and a chapter card names the next stop. Letters. Wren is a courier, so deliveries matter to the story. A mystery. Someone has been leaving notes behind the clocks, signed with a single letter. You can try to work out who. The two parts Part Chapters What it is Part One 1 to 10 From Wicklow Halt to the Hour Road. Part Two 11 onward (11 to 14 playable today) New regions, plus side activities: cooking, fishing, a card game, an arena and hunts. Each region has a chapter page without spoilers, and a separate plot page for after you have played it. A shared world The game is set in the same world as the other BlairsLab games. A few places you pass appear in those games too, for example the walled town of Belcourt, the lamplit Wayward Road, the valley with the keeper's bell, and the foot of a very tall tower on the High Moor. You don't need to have played the others. More about the setting is on The Evenwold and the Rust , and the people you meet are on People of the roads . Next From the same world

x: Home The Roads Between Start here Getting started Getting started Everything you need for your first hour - how a new game begins, what to do on the road, resting, saving and money. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page How a new game begins The first ten minutes Money Resting and saving If you lose The five-minute version of the rules First tips How a new game begins A new game starts in Wren's room above the Wicklow post office, with Wren alone, three Tonics and 30 Marks. Corwin joins in Chapter 1, and the rest of the party gathers as the chapters go on. The game is played in landscape. The first ten minutes Talk to everyone. Many people tell you where to go next, and a few give you errands. Walk east. The road from Wicklow Halt leads to your first fights and your first save point. Details are on Wicklow Halt and the Old Cutting . Fight small things first. Rust shows on the map, so you can pick fights you can win and gain a level or two before the first boss. Keep supplies. A few Tonics (heal HP) and Oil Cans (cure Rusting and Seized) are worth having in the bag at all times. Money Marks are the money of the roads. You earn them from beaten Rust, some chests and story rewards, and spend them on: items in shops (see Shops ), a bed at an inn (10 Marks), crafting at a smith, from Chapter 4 (see Growth and crafting ), resetting a Mainspring board (25 Marks). Resting and saving The game saves whenever you go through a door . You can also save by hand from the Save page, but only at a save point : a small clock face set in a wall (a save clock ), a camp by the road, or a bed . Resting at a bed, camp or save clock heals everyone completely (HP and Wind) and saves the game. A rest at a camp can also play a campfire talk between two friends, which builds their bond. After a rest most Rust come back. The exceptions are Rust that roam close to a save clock or camp, which stay beaten, and one-off guards and bosses, which never return. Rest before every boss, and again before you leave a region. If you lose Losing a fight costs you nothing but time. The game offers to try the battle again or to go back to your last save . If a fight feels hopeless, read Training and difficulty . The five-minute version of the rules Rust is visible and chases you when it notices you. Touching it starts a fight; there are no random encounters. In a fight, each hero has their own turn clock. A bar at the top shows who acts next. Skills cost Wind . Plain attacks are free. Wind comes back with rests, items and some meals. Every hero has a Chime meter that fills as you act and as you are hit. A full Chime is a strong free move. The four elements, Spark , Frost , Tide and Gale , beat different kinds of Rust. The moth's Seek Light shows each foe's weakness. See Elements and statuses . You cannot run from a boss. First tips Check the Almanac and Moth pages in the menu whenever something new happens. Bring a mix of elements. Spark beats most of what you meet early; Frost and Tide beat the rest. Hidden chests need the moth's Seek Light and show themselves when you walk close. Use Guard: it halves the damage you take and brings your next turn sooner. More tips are on FAQ and tips , and the controls are on Controls and menus . Previous From the same world Next Training and difficulty

s: Why the bosses are hard, why most players lose the first time, and how a few extra fights and the difficulty setting fix it.
x: Home The Roads Between Start here Training and difficulty Training and difficulty Why the bosses are hard, why most players lose the first time, and how a few extra fights and the difficulty setting fix it. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Why bosses feel hard A few extra fights Learning a boss Difficulty settings Quick checklist before a boss The bosses in The Roads Between are hard. If you only fight what stands in your way, you will usually reach each boss a little under-levelled, and most players lose a boss fight the first time. That is intended, and a few extra fights fix it. Why bosses feel hard Bosses are tuned so that a party which fights only what is on its path loses most first attempts. Ordinary Rust are tuned too. A party at about the right level for a region takes a fair amount of damage from each group and loses an occasional fight. A party a couple of levels under loses more of them. Heroes gain a small extra power bonus for every level above 10, so late levels matter more than they look. A few extra fights After about three more levels , which is roughly a dozen extra group fights , a boss becomes a fair fight. You don't need to grind for hours. Ways to train: Clear the region properly. Fight the Rust you walk past, not only the ones in the way. Rest, then fight again. Most Rust return after a rest, apart from those that roam close to a save clock or a camp. Take the optional demi-boss (elite) of each chapter. It is fought once and pays a large share of XP, Marks and drops. Spend your Mainspring points and keep your gear up to date at the local shop. See Growth and crafting . Bring the right element. A weakness makes a big difference. See Elements and statuses . Tip Losing is cheap. Try the battle again, watch what the boss does, and change one thing: bring a different element, heal sooner, or Guard when you see a BIG move coming. Learning a boss Bosses follow a fixed pattern of moves rather than choosing at random, so you can learn them. A move marked BIG is shown by the moth's Glow a turn before it lands. Guard, or keep a hero healthy enough to take it. The moth's Seek shows weaknesses, and Ottoline's Read shows what every foe will do next. You cannot flee from a boss. Difficulty settings Change it any time in Settings . Setting What it means Story Gentle battles: the Rust hits softer and falls faster. For people who want the story. Normal The standard setting. You will want to fight a few extra things along the way to keep up with each boss. Hard The Rust hits harder and takes longer to stop. If a boss will not budge, switching to Story for one fight is fine. The story doesn't change. Quick checklist before a boss Rested at a bed, camp or save clock. A few Tonics, Wind Draughts and an Oil Can or two in the bag. The right element on hand: check the boss's weakness on Bosses and hunts if you do not mind spoilers. Every hero's Mainspring points spent. Previous Getting started Next Controls and menus

Updated 11 November 2026 On this page On a phone or tablet On a computer The menu In battle The screen On a phone or tablet Walk. Put your thumb down on the left side of the screen and drag in the direction you want to go. The drag works like a thumbstick, so it never needs to be precise. Action button. The round button on the right. Its label changes to match what is in front of the party: Talk (a person), Open (a chest), Read (a sign or notice), Rest (a bed, a camp or a save clock) or Look (anything else). It is dimmed when there is nothing to use. Menu. The Menu button at the top left. Minimap. A small north-up map with a compass sits in a corner. Tap it for a larger view with a legend. You can switch it off in Settings. On a computer Walk with WASD or the arrow keys , or hold the mouse button and drag. Space , Enter or E is the action button. Escape opens and closes the menu. The menu The menu has eight pages. Page What it is for Party Each hero's stats, skills and bonds. Items The bag: heal, restore Wind, cure, revive or throw things. Equip One weapon, one coat and two trinkets per hero. See Weapons and Coats and trinkets . Mainspring The skill boards, spent with the points you earn for each level. See Growth and crafting . Moth The moth's Lights. See The moth's Lights . Almanac The Clock Almanac records every kind of Rust you have met, the first time you fight it. It also keeps your fishing catch log once you have started fishing. Settings Difficulty, the minimap and other options. Save Save by hand. Only works at a bed, camp or save clock. In battle The turn-order bar at the top shows who acts next. On your turn you choose from Attack , Skill , Item , Guard , Chime , Chain , Flee and, once the moth has learned them, Moth . Every command is explained on Battle basics . The screen Doors and exits take you between maps. A door you have just come through does not fire again until you step out and back in. Chests, signs and people show nothing until you stand next to them; the action button then names what you can do. A dark place is lit by the moth's Glow , and some sealed doors need its Kindle . s: How the maps work, how Rust behaves, where you can rest and save, and the barge, rail-cart and balloon that speed up travel.
x: Home The Roads Between How to play Exploring, saving and travel Exploring, saving and travel How the maps work, how Rust behaves, where you can rest and save, and the barge, rail-cart and balloon that speed up travel. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Walking the world Rust on the map Hidden things Resting and saving Fast travel Marks, shops and the smith Side stories and errands Walking the world You walk the whole party as one group; the other heroes follow behind. Towns, roads and dungeons are separate maps joined by doors and exits . Each region's page under Chapters lists its maps, people, shops and save points. Rust on the map Rust wanders the maps and notices you from a few tiles away . It chases you, and touching it starts a fight. There are no random battles . You can see a fight coming and decide whether to take it. Some Rust stand guard and do not move. Others are one-off fights that never return. When you escape from a fight, that Rust is dazed for a moment so you can get away. Each chapter also has an optional elite (a demi-boss) walking at the far side of some map with two smaller kin. It is fought once and pays well. See Bestiary . Hidden things Some chests are hidden. They only show themselves once the moth has learned Seek (from Chapter 2) and you walk close. Dark passages show in the moth's Glow , and some sealed doors need its Kindle . See The moth's Lights . Resting and saving Place What it does Bed Rest, heal everyone fully (HP and Wind) and save. Camp The same, and the rest can play a campfire talk between two friends, which builds their bond. Save clock A small clock face set in a wall. The same as a camp. Inn A bed for a few Marks (10 Marks). The game also saves automatically whenever you go through a door. You can only save by hand from the Save page at a bed, camp or save clock; elsewhere the page tells you that you cannot save there. After a rest, most Rust come back. The exceptions are Rust that roam close to a save clock or camp (within about eight tiles): those stay beaten, so standing by a save clock is not a way to farm fights. This is how you train for a boss; see Training and difficulty . Fast travel As the story hands you each way of getting about, fast travel opens. A stop only works once you have visited it. Way of travel Where it takes you The barge , Bett's Kittiwake (from Chapter 5) Between moorings: The Hopfields Lock, Tollbridge Wharf, Saltmarsh Wharf and Brindle Quay. The clockwork rail-cart (from Chapter 7) Between old branch-line stations: Wicklow Halt, Hollowmere Halt, Moor Halt and Cinder Works Halt. The balloon (from Chapter 9) Between high places: the Cinder Works and the Hour Road. Marks, shops and the smith You earn Marks from fights, chests and story rewards, and spend them at shops and at the smith's forge (from Chapter 4). A bed at an inn costs 10 Marks. Anything with a price can be sold back, but key items such as letters and keys cannot. Side stories and errands Most towns have a handful of optional errands: a delivery, a problem to solve, a lost thing to find. They pay in Marks and items and often in a cooking recipe. The region pages under Chapters list them. Previous Controls and menus Next Battle basics

s: How fights work - the turn-order bar, Wind, Guard, Chimes, statuses, flee rules and what you get for winning.
x: Home The Roads Between How to play Battle basics Battle basics How fights work - the turn-order bar, Wind, Guard, Chimes, statuses, flee rules and what you get for winning. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The basics What you can do on your turn Bending the turn order Wind Guard Rewind Chimes Foes and their moves Damage, in plain words After a win The basics A battle starts when you touch a roaming Rust. Up to four heroes fight, against one or more Rust. Fights run on a visible turn-order bar . Nobody waits for a round: every fighter has their own clock, and whoever's next turn comes soonest acts. A fighter's wait between turns shrinks as their Speed rises. You win when every Rust has fallen, and lose when all your heroes have. Losing offers try the battle again or back to your last save . You cannot flee from a boss . Elsewhere, fleeing can fail; the chance is better when your party is faster than the Rust. Rust choose their next move as soon as they finish one . That is why the moth's Glow can show a big move a turn before it lands. What you can do on your turn Command What it does Attack A plain hit with your weapon. Free. Skill A skill from your list, paid for in Wind . Item Use something from the bag: heal, restore Wind, cure, revive, or throw a jar at a foe. Guard Brace: you take half damage until your next turn, and your next turn also comes sooner. Chime Your limit move, free, but only when the Chime meter is full. Chain A move two friends do together (see Bonds, Chains and Chimes ). Flee Try to run (not from bosses). Moth The moth's own moves, free, once per battle each, as it learns them. See The moth's Lights . Bending the turn order The turn-order bar shows the next several turns as things stand. Many skills bend it. Effect Examples What happens Hurry Wren's Hurry, the moth's Kindle A friend goes next (Hurry) or straight after this turn (Kindle). Delay Corwin's Delay A foe is pushed back down the order. Sooner Quick Step, Rope Swing, Shortcut and others The caster's next turn comes sooner. Later Bett's Heave A big hit, but the caster's next turn comes a little later. Hurried / Slowed Express, Undertow, Rime and others A status that shrinks or stretches a fighter's wait for a while. Rewind Corwin Undoes the last thing a foe did. Read Ottoline Shows what every foe will do next, for the whole battle. Wind Wind is the energy skills cost. Each hero has a pool that grows with level. Basic attacks cost nothing. Wind comes back at a rest , from items such as the Wind Draught, from some meals, and from Mainspring nodes that give a few Wind back each turn. It does not otherwise regenerate during a fight. Guard Guard halves the damage you take until your next turn and shortens your wait for it. Some skills Guard others instead: Bett's Bulwark guards every friend, and her Drop Anchor makes foes go for her for a while. Some Mainspring nodes start every battle already Guarded. Rewind Corwin's Rewind (from level 2) undoes the last thing a foe did: damage, statuses and its place in the order. It works once a battle. It can grow stronger later in the story. In a few places where time is held , plain Rewind does nothing; the game tells you when that applies. Chimes Each hero has a Chime meter. It fills a little every time you act and a little every time you are hit; Mainspring nodes make it fill faster. When it is full you can use the hero's Chime : a strong, free limit move that spends the whole meter. Each hero's Chime is listed on the

s: Spark, Frost, Tide, Gale and plain Gear - what each is good against - and every status that can land on a fighter.
x: Home The Roads Between How to play Elements and statuses Elements and statuses Spark, Frost, Tide, Gale and plain Gear - what each is good against - and every status that can land on a fighter. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Elements Statuses Cures at a glance Elements There are four elements, plus plain hits. Element Where it comes from Notes Spark Corwin's Arc, Pip's Flare, Spark Jars and Storm Jars "A crackle of Spark from the tuning rod. The Rust hates it." Most Rust early in the game are weak to Spark. Frost Ottoline's Rime and Hard Frost, Frost Flasks "A breath of Frost. Hot Rust hates it." Furnaces, boilers and anything running hot. Tide Bett's Undertow and Bow Wave, Brine Flasks Water. Good against gnats, kites, pickers, tubs, mowers and cairns. Gale A wind element that comes into play in Chapter 12 Wind never misses, and fliers cannot dodge it. Rust that sails or flaps hates it. Gear (plain) Ordinary weapon hits and most plain skills A hit with no element is "plain". A Rust that resists Gear also resists ordinary weapon hits. Each Rust lists what it is weak to and what it resists in the Bestiary . A weak hit does about half again as much damage; a resisted hit does clearly less. The moth's Seek Light shows each foe's weakness in battle. See The moth's Lights . Ottoline's Expose makes a foe take extra damage from everything. Elemental jars and flasks are a quick way to carry an element you do not have on hand. See Consumables . Tip Bring a mix. A party with one Spark hero, one Frost hero and one Tide hero covers nearly everything on the early roads. Statuses Status Effect Rusting Hurts a little each turn (a small share of the fighter's maximum HP). Cured by Oil Cans, Poultice, Thaw and similar. Seized Skips a turn. Cured by the same items. The moth's Wake can stop the first one each battle. Slowed The fighter's wait between turns is stretched. Hurried The wait is shrunk. Guarded Takes half damage until the fighter's next turn. Dazed Attacks miss about half the time. Taunting Foes tend to attack this fighter (Bett's Drop Anchor). Exposed Takes about a third more damage (Ottoline's Expose, Hard Frost, Thermal Shock, Cold Post). Cures at a glance Problem Cure Rusting and Seized Oil Can (10 Marks), Poultice, Thaw and similar healing skills, Pepper Soup Fallen hero Smelling Salts (40 Marks) Low HP Tonic and its bigger relatives; see Consumables Low Wind Wind Draught (20 Marks), some meals Previous Battle basics Next Bonds, Chains and Chimes

x: Home The Roads Between How to play Bonds, Chains and Chimes Bonds, Chains and Chimes How friendships build in camp and battle, the team moves they unlock, and each hero's limit move. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Chimes Bonds Chains and Duets Chimes Each hero has a Chime meter. It fills a little every time you act and a little every time you are hit; some Mainspring nodes make it fill faster. When it is full you can use the hero's Chime : a strong, free limit move that spends the whole meter. Hero Chime What it does Wren Special Delivery A flying strike through every foe (2.2x Attack). Corwin Hour Hand Spark across every foe (2x Mind), with an 80% chance to slow them for 3 turns. Bett Bow Wave A wall of Tide across every foe (2x Attack), with a 30% chance to Seize them for a turn. Ottoline Hard Frost Frost across every foe (1.9x Mind), with a 70% chance to Expose them for 2 turns. Senn Last Post One delivery nobody can refuse: 3.4x Attack on a single foe. Pip Steeplejack A rain of shot on every foe (2.1x Attack) that never misses. Bonds Bonds build between two friends from campfire talks, story scenes and fighting together. There are five Bond levels: Bond level Points needed 1 4 2 12 3 24 4 40 5 60 Campfire talks are the best source of points: rest at a camp, and a talk may play between two friends you have not heard from yet. Fighting side by side also adds a little. Chains and Duets A Chain is two friends acting as one. It opens at Bond level 2 . It costs 4 Wind each , hits with the stronger of the two heroes plus half of the weaker's power, and the partner gives up their next turn. If both Chimes are full , the Chain becomes a Duet : it costs no Wind, hits half again as hard , and spends both Chimes. Chain Partners Bond Targets What it does Charged Delivery Wren and Corwin 2 all foes Spark, 1.7x Mind. Wren carries Corwin's Spark through every foe. Tidal Rush Wren and Bett 2 one foe Tide, 3x Attack, always slows the foe for 3 turns. Steam Burst Corwin and Bett 2 all foes Tide, 1.4x Mind, 60% chance to Daze for 2 turns. Thermal Shock Corwin and Ottoline 2 all foes Frost, 1.5x Mind, always Exposes for 2 turns. Ice Floe Bett and Ottoline 2 one foe Frost, 2.6x Attack, 60% chance to Seize for a turn. Ice Bulwark Bett and Ottoline 4 all friends Guards everyone for a turn and cures Rusting and Seized. Cold Post Wren and Ottoline 2 one foe Frost, 2.4x Attack, always Exposes for 3 turns. There is a Chain for every pairing of the four main heroes, and Bett and Ottoline get a second one at Bond level 4. Later heroes bring Chains of their own; see their pages under The party . Tip Keep some Wind in reserve for Chains, and rest at camps often so more campfire talks play. Previous Elements and statuses Next The lantern moth and its Lights

s: The moth never fights, but its six Lights open the map and give each battle a helping hand.
x: Home The Roads Between How to play The lantern moth and its Lights The lantern moth and its Lights The moth never fights, but its six Lights open the map and give each battle a helping hand. Updated 11 November 2026 A small moth made of soft golden light found Wren on the first page of the story and will not leave. It never attacks . It learns Lights as the chapters go by, and each one helps you on the map and in battle. The Moth page in the menu lists what it knows. Light Learned On the map In battle Glow Chapter 1 Lights dark places and shows hidden passages. Glows on a foe about to make a BIG move, a turn early. Seek Chapter 2 Points toward hidden treasure: hidden chests show themselves when you come close. Shows what each Rust is weak to. Kindle Chapter 4 Lights old lamps to open sealed doors. Once per fight and free: a friend you choose goes straight after the current turn. Wake Chapter 6 Wakes frozen people for a moment. Once per fight: the first time a hero would be Seized, the moth wakes them instead. Guide Chapter 8 Leads the way through fog and mazes. Shows what every Rust will do next. Dawn Chapter 10 A battle Light. Once per fight and free: heals every friend a little and clears Rusting, Seized, Dazed and Slowed. Using the Lights In battle the moth's moves sit under Moth in the command list, once learned. Kindle and Dawn are free, once per battle each. Glow and Guide work on their own, so you don't choose them. Seek is what makes hidden chests show up and shows a Rust's weakness in the fight. If you missed a chest, come back after Chapter 2. Tip Use Kindle on a hero whose Chime is full, or whose next skill will turn the fight. Use Dawn when two or three friends are hurt, or when a status has landed on several of them. x: Home The Roads Between How to play Growth and crafting Growth and crafting Levels, XP, the Mainspring boards, gear and what the smith can make from Rust Scrap. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page Levels and XP Mainspring boards Gear Crafting with Rust Scrap The Almanac Levels and XP Heroes start at level 1 (new heroes join at a set level, or at the party leader's level) and can reach level 60 . Every battle gives XP to the whole party. The XP needed for the next level grows steadily: level 1 to 2 needs 10 XP, level 10 to 11 needs 282, level 30 to 31 needs 1,386 and level 59 to 60 needs 3,696. A hero who is knocked out still gets half the XP, and a hero behind the party's highest level catches up faster , so a hero who keeps falling does not drift further behind. A level-up raises HP, Wind, Attack, Defence, Mind and Speed by the hero's own growth rates, and may teach a new skill . Skill levels are on each hero's page under The party . A few skills are taught by the story instead. Heroes also gain a small power bonus for every level above 10. The game is tuned so that fighting only what stands in your way leaves you a little short at each boss, and a few extra fights close the gap. See Training and difficulty . Mainspring boards Each of the four main heroes has a Mainspring board (Menu, then Mainspring): two branches , each with five nodes . A hero earns one point per level after the first and spends them on nodes, which cost 1 to 3 points. Nodes in a branch are bought in order, and you may pick freely between branches. Wren's Courier branch makes her faster and gives her a first turn that comes early; her Guardian of the Post branch makes her sturdier. Corwin's branches are Horologist (Spark) and Repairer (healing and durability). Bett's are Bargewoman and Tidewater , and Ottoline's are Natural Philosopher (Frost) and Field Physician . Nodes give stats or a passive : a first turn that comes early, 2 Wind back every turn, starting each fight Guarded, a chance to strike back, harder hits for one element, a faster Chime, or more critical hits. Resetting a board costs 25 Marks , so you can try a different path. Guest heroes have no board. Every node is listed on The Mainspring boards . Gear Each hero wears one weapon , one coat and two trinkets (Menu, then Equip). A weapon must match the hero's weapon kind: Wren uses blades, Corwin rods, Bett hooks, Ottoline lenses, Senn openers, Pip slings. Gear adds to Attack, Defence, Mind or Speed. Weapons and coats come from shops, chests, Rust drops and the smith. Trinkets are mostly the small Cogs that a smith makes. These are not the Cogs card game . Everything with a price can be sold. Key items cannot. Full lists: Weapons , Coats and trinkets , Shops . Crafting with Rust Scrap Every beaten Rust leaves Rust Scrap (bigger Rust leave more; bosses leave a fixed amount). From Chapter 4 the smith at Cobb's Forge in Lowdelve has a Make page that turns Scrap plus Marks into things you cannot buy: Makes Rust Scrap Marks Effect Quick Cog 6 60 Speed +3 Sturdy Cog 6 60 Defence +4 Keen Cog 6 60 Attack +3, Speed +1 Bright Cog 6 60 Mind +4 Frost Flask (makes 2) 3 20 Deals 60 Frost damage to a foe Master Cog 18 200 +2 to every stat Tip Each hero has two trinket slots, so a pair of Cogs on everyone is a cheap boost before a boss. How it works A recipe turns ingredients (ordinary items: crops, fish, Rust drops) into a meal , which is also an ordinary item. You can cook a recipe once you know it. The first three recipes come from Mrs Crumb. Others are taught by side stories, such as Nan Marsh's duff. A meal either heals (eaten from the bag or in battle) or gives the whole party a buff for the next battle . A buff meal is eaten outside battle and lasts until the next fight. s: A short timing minigame at marked spots on the quay, twelve fish to catch, a catch log and meals made from the haul.
x: Home The Roads Between How to play Fishing Fishing A short timing minigame at marked spots on the quay, twelve fish to catch, a catch log and meals made from the haul. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page How a cast works A better rod The fish Where to fish Fishing opens in Chapter 12, at Brindle Quay . Read the Angling Notice by the Harbour Steps and you are given a Quay Rod ; until then the fishing posts do nothing. Every fish you land is an ordinary item: sell it, eat it or cook it. The Almanac in the menu keeps a catch log of every fish you have landed. How a cast works Wait for the dip. Cast at a marked fishing spot and wait for a bite. Tugging too soon puts the fish on guard, and doing it twice scares them off. Strike. When you see "A bite!" tap at once. You get only a short window, and rarer fish give you less time. Reel. A marker slides back and forth. Tap when it is inside the green zone. Rarer fish need more good taps, and the marker moves faster. Don't slip. Three taps outside the zone and the line snaps. Dithering too long lets the fish go, and a cast that nobody taps times out. Tip Wait for the dip. A fish that spooks is gone for the cast, but you only lose a few seconds. A better rod A side story at the Quay leads to the Regatta Rod : fish bite more readily, you get longer to strike, and the rare ones come a little more often. The fish Fish Rarity Notes Quay Sprat Common Everywhere, and always in a hurry. Silver Herring Common The Quay's own. Caught off the steps by the thousand. s: A small card game of winding your clock to 12 before your opponent does, with a ladder of opponents in Candlewick and rare cards as prizes.
x: Home The Roads Between How to play Cogs, the card game Cogs, the card game A small card game of winding your clock to 12 before your opponent does, with a ladder of opponents in Candlewick and rare cards as prizes. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The rules in plain language The cards and your deck The ladder in Candlewick How the opponents play Cogs is an optional two-player card game: a small deck-building game against people you meet on the roads, with a ladder of opponents and rare cards as prizes. It is taught in Chapter 14, at the corner table in Candlewick , by Aunty Ratchet , who also keeps the ladder. Note Cogs is not the same as the small gear-shaped trinkets a smith makes, which are also called cogs. See the Glossary . The rules in plain language The aim. Each player has a clock with 12 hours . Wind yours round to 12 before the other player does. Decks. A deck is exactly 20 cards : at most 2 of any card, and only 1 of any rare. You start with 4 cards in hand (the player going second starts with one extra). A hand holds up to 7 ; a card drawn into a full hand is lost. A turn. You draw a card, then you have Wind to spend: 1 on your first turn, 2 on your second, and so on up to 5. Play any cards you can afford (each costs Wind), in any order, then end your turn. Unspent Wind is lost. Card kinds. - Gears wind your clock on. - Springs give you Wind, so they pay for the dearer cards. - Escapements push the other clock back. - Tricks are all effect. Effects (at most one per card, after its main job): Draw , Delay (the foe has less Wind next turn, never below 1), Hurry (wind your clock on more), Steal (take hours from the foe's clock to yours), Rewind (undo up to that many of the hours the foe wound on during their last turn) and Guard (soaks up the next hours you would lose from a push, a steal or a rewind; you can hold at most 4). Winning. The moment your clock reaches 12 you win. If a player cannot draw because their deck has run dry, the game ends and whoever is further round wins (a tie goes to the player who went second). A game also stops after 60 turns in total on the same rule. The cards and your deck There are 40 cards : 18 common, 14 uncommon and 8 rare. The whole list is on Cogs cards . You start with a deck of two each of Pocket Cog, Brass Cog, Great Cog, Tick Wheel, Coil Spring, Sticky Pawl, Catch Pin, Oil Can, Brass Shield and Winder's Key. You build and change your deck on the deck screen, from the cards you own. You get more cards from: Beating opponents. The first win over each pays Marks and a card. Beating Rust. About 18 percent of fights can leave a card behind. The ladder in Candlewick Each opponent must be beaten to challenge the next, and only the first win over each pays. Beaten opponents can be played again for fun but pay nothing more. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page How it works The ladder The duellists The Arena Hand, then Tin Tolliver, Mags Mangle, Lord Tick, Brisk Bridget, The Salt Duchess, Captain Gnash, Old Hollis Hardhand, Madam Chime, The Glass Knight and Sir Highsun. The Arena opens in Chapter 13, at Saltglass . It is an optional ladder of ten ranked clockwork duels . You never have to enter and the story doesn't need it, but it tests a party well and pays in Marks and gear you can't buy. How it works The Arena opens once you have spoken to Marshal Brass , and the rank board lists the ten fighters. Rank 1 is open to you at once. To challenge rank n , you must have beaten ranks 1 to n minus 1. Each rank is a hard duel against a named fighter. Use any party you like. The first win of a rank pays once : Marks, and at every second rank a piece of gear that cannot be bought. A beaten rank can be fought again for a small purse, but only the first three rematches of each rank pay anything. After that it is for honour. Duellists give no XP, Marks, Rust Scrap or drops , so the Arena cannot be farmed. Losing costs nothing. The game restores the moment before the fight, and you can try again. The level shown below is only a guide to when a steady party finds the rank a fair fight. You can challenge a rank at any level. s: Optional named Rust at the end of a clue chain - how to start one from an inn's notice board, and what each of the four so far is weak to.
x: Home The Roads Between How to play Hunts Hunts Optional named Rust at the end of a clue chain - how to start one from an inn's notice board, and what each of the four so far is weak to. Updated 11 November 2026 A hunt is an optional chase after a named Rust, much bigger and meaner than anything on the road. Each chapter from 11 to 14 has one. You never have to take one up, and they are among the hardest fights in the game, so come back for them when you have levelled. How a hunt works Read the notice board at the region's inn. It tells you who is being hunted and starts the chase. Follow three clues. Talk to the people the board and each clue point you to, and check the trail signs in the wild. The last trail sign leads to the Rust's lair. Fight. The named Rust only shows on the map once the chase has led you there. It does not chase you, it is a one-off, and it follows a fixed pattern of moves like a boss. You cannot flee from it. Collect. You earn a large share of XP and Marks, plus a healing item that is always dropped. The four hunts so far Chapter Hunt Board at Where it lurks Weak to 11 The Whistling Kettle The Gleaner's Rest, Larkhill The Rolling Downs Frost, Tide 12 Old Clanger The Bunting and Anchor, Brindle Quay Brindle Quay Spark, Gale 13 Old Sunstruck The Parasol Inn, Saltglass Saltglass Fair Frost, Tide 14 The Runaway Cake The Wick and Wax, Candlewick The Lantern Fields Tide, Gale Hunt Rust hit far harder than that chapter's boss (their Attack and Mind are well above it), so go in trained. The stats and moves are on Bosses and hunts , with spoilers for the other bosses on that page. Tip A hunt is a good use of a stack of Frost Flasks, Storm Jars and Hot Broths. Rest at the nearest camp or save clock first, then bring every cure you own: hunts love Rusting, Slowed and Seized. Previous The Saltglass Arena Next The party

s: The world of the game - its roads, its clocks, and the clockwork creatures gone to rust that you meet on them.
x: Home The Roads Between World The Evenwold and the Rust The Evenwold and the Rust The world of the game - its roads, its clocks, and the clockwork creatures gone to rust that you meet on them. Updated 11 November 2026 On this page The Evenwold The places A shared world The Rust The Evenwold The Evenwold is the name of the world in the story: villages, towns and works joined by old roads, rail-cuts and canals. Each town keeps its own clock. When a clock stops, so does everything that was keeping time with it, and everyone who was outside under its face stops with it. The clocks that stopped on the first morning all read 6:12 , and you will see that time on nearly every wall. Places stopped later, in the second half of the story, keep their own hours. The places The game starts at the green edge of the world and the weather gets stranger from there. Each region has its own page. Chapter Region 1 Wicklow Halt and the Old Cutting : a station village and a disused railway tunnel 2 The Hopfields and the Wayward Light : hop gardens, a canal lock and a lamp road 3 Tollbridge and Belcourt : a bridge town and a walled hill town 4 Lowdelve and the Underway : a mining valley and the dark workings below it 5 Saltmarsh Wharf : a harbour town in the fog 6 The Valley and the Glasshouse Estate 7 Hollowmere : a lake with a village under it 8 The High Moor : snow, fog and standing stones 9 The Cinder Works : a cold foundry town 10 The Hour Road : the road to the last clock 11 Larkhill : a village at an endless supper 12 Brindle Quay : a harbour of bunting 13 Saltglass : a white salt flat at noon 14 Candlewick : a lantern town on a wedding evening A shared world Every BlairsLab game is set in the Evenwold. Places like Belcourt, the lamplit Wayward Road, the valley with the keeper's bell and the foot of a very tall tower on the High Moor appear in the others too. You don't need to have played them. The Rust The Rust is what has gone wrong with the clocks: clockwork creatures, from beetles and gnats to scarecrows, hornets, boats and whole machines, gone to rust. The game never explains what the Rust is or where it comes from. You see Rust on the maps and can pick your fights. There are no random battles. Each kind has its own look, moves, weaknesses and drops. They are catalogued in the Bestiary . Each chapter has an optional elite , a tougher version of one of its ordinary Rust, escorted by two smaller kin. Bosses are named Rust, each a machine that has taken over a clock. They are on their own page, which has spoilers: Bosses and hunts . Previous Sabine Averill Next People of the roads

Updated 11 November 2026 On this page At a glance The Saltglass Arena Rust here Chests and secrets Side stories and errands Hunt Tips East of the Quay the bunting runs out and the ground turns to white salt. Saltglass is flat salt as far as you can see, with a Fair in the middle of it: flags, striped awnings, a roundabout of folding chairs and stalls selling ice and lemonade. It is always noon, so every shadow points straight down and none of them move. Saltglass, where it is always noon Heat is the new thing here. Out in the open the sun builds up on your party, and a heat pulse costs everyone a little health (never all of it). Parasols and boardwalks are shade, and stepping under one clears the heat. Plan your walks from one patch of shade to the next. The Porter, trunk under each arm Place guide: Wicklow Halt and the Old Cutting . Next: Chapter 2 plot and boss . What happens In forty years the 6:12 to Tollbridge has never been late. This morning it did not come at all. Wren notices that Aunt Agnes's kettle has gone quiet, and when she turns round Agnes is standing at the counter with her stamp raised, warm but perfectly still. A small moth made of soft light taps at the window, flies off towards the shop and back, and waits until Wren follows. It gives her the first of its Lights, Glow. Outside, everyone who was in the open is frozen where they stood, and the station clock has stopped at twelve minutes past six. By the platform Wren meets a nervous clockmaker called Corwin, who fell asleep in the waiting room after the last train. He explains that anyone out under the clock's face when it stopped stopped with it, and that somebody has pulled the escapement (the part that lets a clock tick) clean out. The moth settles on the clock and then flies a slow loop to the east. Corwin spots rust-marked scrape marks along the platform heading the same way, towards the Old Cutting, and he can't leave a broken clock alone. He joins Wren. The two follow the road east and climb into the disused tunnel, where the moth's Glow reveals a hidden way through the wall. At the far end stands the station's old luggage porter, clockwork and rusted through, with a trunk under each arm. It demands tickets, and Wren has to fight it. When it is beaten it sets its trunks down gently, as if putting them on a rack, and Corwin tells it to rest. Wren gets the Station Escapement back. Back at the Halt, Corwin fits it and the moth circles the clock face once. The pendulum swings and the village starts again: a loaf lands in a basket, a broom finishes its sweep, a kettle boils somewhere. Old Jory the stationmaster is baffled that it is nearly half past nine. Tucked behind the clock face is an envelope addressed "To whoever mends the clocks". The note inside asks the finder to stop: everything that ticks will one day end, let them rest, let the world rest. It is signed only "S." Corwin says quietly that whoever wrote it means to stop more clocks. The moth drifts out along the road and waits for them. The oak has come down across the Tollbridge road, so Corwin suggests the old path north through the Hopfields instead. Wren wants to see Aunt Agnes first, and Agnes sends her off on her first real round with three letters for the Hopfields. Party and moth Joins: Corwin (level 2). Nobody leaves. Moth Light: Glow (Light 1), at the start. It lights dark places, shows hidden ways, and in battle shows a BIG move a turn early. Letters: Aunt Agnes gives you the Hopfields Post, three letters to deliver in Chapter 2. Boss: The Porter The station's old porter, taken by the Rust. It is the gentlest boss in the game, but you only have Wren and Corwin, so don't take it lightly. These are base

What happens The path north brings Wren and Corwin into the Hopfields, where every picker stands frozen mid-reach. The moth drifts towards the canal and a barge sitting dead in the water. Up from below deck comes Bett Marsh, owner of the Kittiwake, who was below when it happened and came up to find everything had stopped. The lock is frozen, the lock-keeper is frozen and her hold of hops is going nowhere. Wren realises that "B. Marsh, barge Kittiwake" is one of the three people on Agnes's list, and hands over a letter from Bett's sister in Saltmarsh. Bett says she will read it later. Then she decides that fixing clocks and fixing her lock are the same job, and joins the party. The lock has its own clock, stopped at twelve minutes past six, with a note behind its face in the same hand as Wicklow's: "Please stop. Let the water rest. It has carried enough. - S." Corwin says it is the same writer. Bett explains that the lock runs off the windmill's pump, so the mill has stopped too. As they talk the light goes amber and then grey, and Bett refuses to go out in the dark. She sends them to the lamp tower on the east road. At the Wayward Light every lamp along the road is burning. The lamplighter lights them all every night: "It's not much. But it keeps the road." Wren delivers the last of her letters, and the moth rises up the tower to the great lamp, circles the flame and comes back shining a little differently. It has learned Seek. The lamplighter lets the party rest until morning, and asks them to tell whoever keeps the bell in the valley that the lamps are lit all the way to the wall. Along the way Mr Greaves, at the Hop Exchange, welcomes Agnes's girl, and with all three letters handed over Wren earns 50 Marks and the line that couriers finish deliveries. In the morning the mill door opens. Inside, the machinery is jammed, and the levers work the hatch to the threshing floor. A beam is carved with a hint: "Sails turn true when the first and the last are set, and the middle is let be." So the first and last levers go on and the middle one stays off. Above, a barn-sized machine beats the empty boards, and Bett recognises old Brindle's thresher, which has been threshing nothing for a week. After the fight its flails slow and it settles with a tired creak. The mill clock still has its escapement this time, only jammed with chaff. The moth circles the face and the pendulum swings. The great sails turn, the pump wakes, the lock fills and the pickers carry on as if nothing had happened. In the clock case is a third note: "Someone will come and mend this one too. Someone always does. You don't understand what you're mending. - S." Corwin goes quiet and admits he has seen that handwriting before. Bett offers to carry the party down the canal past the fallen oak. Lock-keeper Brindle

What happens The Kittiwake ties up at Tollbridge and Bett says she is staying put until the town is sorted. The toll gates are shut, and the toll clock above them has stopped at twelve minutes past six again. People from both banks are frozen on the bridge, and from the rooftops Wren sees a city to the north standing perfectly still in the rain. "Is that the city? I thought it was a story," she says. Corwin tells her it is real, but nobody goes in. The two councils are no help: Councillor Pell insists it is the Lower Bank's clock and the Lower Bank's fault, while the notice on the other hall says the exact opposite. At the post office Wren meets Senn, a courier from the city, sorting thirty years of dead letters. He came out across the edge with a letter for the belfry at Belcourt and the road has been stuck ever since. He turns over a yellowed envelope addressed only "A., Hollowmere", with no street and no surname. Hollowmere, he says, is under a lake now. Wren cannot let it lie: somebody wrote it and somebody should get it, so she promises to find A. Senn gives her the letter, calls her "postie", and offers to walk with the party to Belcourt. Postmaster Oakes, who knows Aunt Agnes, offers Wren the courier's exam: four parcels, two for each bank. The road climbs to Belcourt, last town before the city, where the Rust comes up the hill every night and every night the town holds the wall. Senn greets Hester Bell like an old friend, and she asks the travellers to help hold the wall tonight. Three waves break against it and the party holds them all. Brother Anselm accepts the belfry letter, and Senn decides to stay at Belcourt and carry the town's post. Hester's grandson Pip Tallow, who watched the fight from the steeple, joins the party when he hears about the stopped toll clock, and Hester asks Wren to bring him back in one piece. What happens The road drops into Lowdelve, where miners, a girl with a birdcage and a man at the pit gate stand frozen. Corwin reasons that the pit clock is down the mine, because a pit rings its bell at the change of shift, and somebody has stopped it at the change. The party descends into the Underway, pitch black, and the moth's light swells, as if telling them to stay close. A voice calls a warning about the third rail, and Wren realises it is a real person. She is Ottoline Ferry, who studies the Rust and means to be the first to find out what it is. She has been down here nine days and never noticed that everyone above has frozen. This was the study of her old teacher, Professor Lisle, who spent eleven years watching the Rust before he packed a bag and walked out, leaving his last three pages missing. Ottoline will not leave without them, and Bett says they will not leave without the pit clock, so Ottoline joins. Once the three pages are found, Ottoline reads them. On day four thousand and six Lisle wrote that he understood the Rust less than on the day he began, that it is not hungry and not cruel, that he did not know what it is, and that he had written down every move it made. "That's it? Eleven years?" Wren suggests that maybe that is a lot. Ottoline realises she can read the Rust the same way, learns Read and keeps his lens. Further in, a passage up to the winding gallery ends at a sealed door, and the miners had sealed their deep doors with lamp-locks, so no flame means no door. Firedamp hisses out of the dark and Ottoline's lamp goes out. After the fight the moth flies to the old miner's lamp beside the door, settles on the wick and the wick catches. It has learned Kindle. The door groans open. Ottoline is astonished, and Wren calls the moth a bit of a show-off. The cage lift rattles down into the Deep Workings, hot and dark, with something huge breathing. Ottoline hears a winding engine still running on nothing. At the bottom it rises on iron legs, a whistle for a mouth and a pick in each fist, calling "SHIFT. CHANGE. ALL. HANDS." Ottoline warns it is as hot as a furnace and Spark will only warm it, so everyone should use Frost. When it is beaten it gives one long tired whistle and quiets. Corwin finds the pit clock packed solid with coal dust and a lump of rust pushed in on purpose. The moth circles it and the hands move. Far above, the shift bell rings and the miners call out their names one by one down the shaft, all accounted for. Behind the pendulum is a fifth note: "Every shift ends. Let this one never begin. - S." Ottoline asks who S. is, and Corwin says it is someone who should know better. Wren presses, and he repeats his promise to explain at Hollowmere, but not down here.
