Corwin tells the party the truth at the chapel clock Back to the place guide: Hollowmere . Previous: Chapter 6 plot . Next: Chapter 8 plot . What happens The road out of the estate comes out above a long still lake with a dam at one end and an old halt on the shore. Wren spots a village under the water. "Hollowmere," says Corwin, and then says nothing for a long time. At the dam house, Mr Haverly explains that the valley was flooded for the water thirty years ago and everyone moved out, but the water never got in. The clockmaker, Master Venn, would not leave, and his wife Marta kept the chapel clock. The water rose to the walls and stopped, like glass. Corwin has gone very pale. Mr Haverly says the lake lets you through if you walk the old road. The water rises on either side and holds above their heads. The village is dry, held exactly as it was thirty years ago. In held time, Corwin's Rewind does nothing. At the post office, one pigeonhole reads "A. VENN, CLOCKMAKER. CHAPEL COTTAGE." It matches the thirty-year-old dead letter in Wren's satchel, addressed "A., Hollowmere". The handwriting matches the name on the chapel clock's plate, "Kept by Marta Venn". The letter is from Marta to her husband, Aldous Venn. Corwin asks everyone to come to the chapel. Corwin's confession. Aldous Venn was Corwin's master for eleven years, the finest clockmaker the guild ever had and the kindest man he knew. When the valley flooded, Aldous stopped the village so the water could not have it, and Marta begged him to let it go. She died the next winter. Aldous decided that, since everything that ticks will end, nothing should tick. Nine years ago he came to the guild with plans for the Stilling Engine, a clock to stop every clock on every road at once, and asked Corwin to help build it. Corwin said no and walked out of the guild. He has let people believe he was thrown out, and tells it that way himself because it is easier to say. The Stillwright, S., is Aldous, and Corwin has known since the windmill. Wren asks why he did not say, and he answers that if he said it aloud it would be true. Bett thanks him for telling them. Ottoline says Aldous is not a monster, just sad, and Corwin calls him the saddest man he ever knew. Wren promises to deliver Marta's letter anyway. Party and moth Nobody joins or leaves. The party is Wren, Corwin, Bett and Ottoline. The moth gains no new Light. Corwin's tuning rod rings by itself, and the moth settles on it. He realises the undoing was Aldous's trick all along. Rewind is reforged as Second Chance : twice a battle, it undoes a foe's last move and steadies everyone, and it works in held time too. Corwin's Bond with Wren, Bett and Ottoline grows, and the Venns' cottage unlocks. What happens The rail-cart climbs onto the High Moor: snow, wind, fog, and a ring of standing stones with a clock set into one of them. Pip Tallow is waiting at the halt. Pip joins the party. Shepherd Ewart says nobody has been up to the stones since the fog came down. Something is in it, and sheep, who go near everything, will not go near. He also talks fondly of the tower down the moor and its lamp. When the party heads for the stones, the fog comes off the high ground all at once, and the quiet comes with it. The wind and the snow stop, and Wren cannot hear her own feet. Something taller than the stones passes through and snowflakes hang still where it goes. Corwin names it: the Hush, which Aldous built to keep things quiet. He shouts for everyone to stay together, and the fog closes in. Wren and Pip are alone. The West Fold. Wren and Pip cannot hear or find the others. The moth glows brighter and flies a little way ahead, then waits, and gains a new Light, Guide. Wren says it has been doing that since the very first morning. They come out at the foot of a tower so tall its top is lost in cloud, with hundreds of small clockwork insects around its base and a lamp burning far above. Wren sends the moth back into the fog for the others. The East Fold. Bett, Corwin and Ottoline are lost in the dark too. Bett offers to carry Ottoline out. Ottoline says she can read the Rust in the dark and Bett cannot, and tells her to hold on to her, for once. After a pause, Bett agrees: "All right. Lead." What happens The balloon sets you down above a road that runs east as far as anyone can see. Ottoline explains that every clock in the Evenwold was once set along it. Hob will wait and a lamp will call him whenever you want a lift. Carvings on the three waystations say that at the first stone the hour was set, that every town keeps its own hour but keeps it for the others, and that at the end of the road there is a clock to be wound kindly, for it is old and has been very patient. In a neat little house sits Master Aldous Venn, the old clockmaker, looking at a clock that does not tick. He greets Corwin with "You came" and takes in the rest of you: a courier, a bargewoman, a scholar and a moth. Wren hands over the dead letter that has been in her satchel since Tollbridge, addressed "A., Hollowmere". It is from Marta, in her own hand. She asks him not to keep it but to keep her, by letting the clocks tick; she would rather be missed than stopped, and asks him to wind something for her on Sunday. Aldous never knew she wrote. He says it was never lost, only kept. He explains why every clock stopped at twelve minutes past six: it was the minute the sluice gates opened above Hollowmere, and he could never choose another. He admits the Stilling Engine cannot be turned off, because he built it so that nothing could. It only holds what the clocks hold. He stilled the first clocks by hand to give it something to grip, so every clock you mended was a grip lost, which is why it is tired. He left a word in each clock for whoever came. He cannot turn the Engine off, but he can wind the Hour Clock with Marta's words in his pocket, and asks to walk with you. The moth's light changes from a lantern's glow to something like the first light of morning. It has learned Dawn , and the road east opens. At the end of the road stands the Hour Clock, hands halted at the top of the hour. In front of it hums the Stilling Engine, one tired note. Corwin says it is not angry, it just cannot stop. Aldous warns that it will try to stop you, "nothing personal". Wren answers that you are not here to break it, only to let the world start again. When it is beaten, the Engine sets itself down in a long exhale of steam, like the Porter did. Aldous walks to the Clock with his brass key and Marta's letter tucked in his sleeve. "I stopped a village once. I told myself it was love. It was only fear with a good reason." Corwin steadies the key, Wren turns it, Aldous covers their hands, and the moth circles the great face. The hands move, and the hour rings along the whole road. Everywhere answers: the station clock at Wicklow Halt and Aunt Agnes's kettle, the mill sails in the Hopfields, the happy arguing on Tollbridge, lamps in the Underway, the tide on time at Saltmarsh, autumn

Your best day, kept." It carries a postmark from a place Corwin insists does not exist. Bett sees a line of glowing people walking east. Ottoline has measured that the Rust is thickest where time is kept as well as where it is stopped. The moth will not come back from the edge of the lamplight. A tall woman with silver hair and a coat with a hundred buttons came through with the lamps and asked why a best day should ever end; the village voted 412 to nothing. The rule is that nobody leaves until the pudding is served and the bell is rung. The pudding bell went down the barn's cellar hatch thirty years ago, so they have seconds, and thirds. Corwin hears dumbwaiters under the table: something feeds it from below. Quince will give you the barn key once you have said hello to Jenny Marsh. Jenny is Bett's sister, who has kept Bett's chair at the Marsh end since she sat down. Half of Saltmarsh followed the lamps. It is not unpleasant, she says, which is the worst of it, but she cannot seem to get up. She replied to Bett's letter and kept the reply in her basket because she did not know where to send it: "Save me a pudding... I read yours nine times. It was the better letter." Below, every jar in the cellar is labelled "Seconds" and the whole place is one clockwork machine, kept by ladles, pie tins and pepper mills. You find the Larder Key and open the iron door. In a chamber as big as the barn stands an oven with a fire in its belly, a pantry around it, and a little brass bell on a hook. Quince panics, then admits he has forgotten what comes after supper. Bett says she can do pudding, and the village makes Marsh Duff together using every fire on the green, passing the sugar the whole length of the table. What happens On the coast road east of Larkhill, a balloon comes down much too fast and lands on a haystack. It is Hob Fenner, the pilot from the Cinder Works. He has spent a week on a hill watching the lamps travel east, and he tells you he would rather be the one who comes along than the one who gives lifts. He asks to join for good. Bett hires him on the spot, on the strength of whether he can cook (he can heat soup). The Long Hope stays tied to the haystack, and a very surprised cow. Brindle Quay is stuck on Regatta Day. The fleet sits frozen on the start line, and Harbour Master Dunnage holds the starting gun and will not fire it. The race cannot begin without the Regatta Cutter, the pilot boat whose sails are the signal, and she has been out on her warm-up lap for thirty years, going faster every circuit. Dunnage admits the rest: once she fires, the race ends, and she has loved this morning for so long. To call the Cutter in you need the three signal flags (Come About, Heave To, Welcome Home). They are locked in the Customs House flag locker. Mr Quillfeather the clerk explains that the locker key is in the vault, in a drawer marked LOST PROPERTY, where he put it for safekeeping and then lost it. You find the key, open the locker, and climb the stair to Keeper Aubrey Pitch, whose daughter Marlin runs a stall in the market. The lighthouse mast that needs the flags stands across a gap where a bridge once was. Hob flies you across in two trips on the Long Hope, and for the first time you see him terrified of the landing and talking himself down ("down, down, there"). He lands on a gallery the size of a tablecloth. You raise the flags, a sail turns out beyond the breakwater, and the first real wind in thirty years stirs the bunting. Ottoline notes that the Rust gathers where time is kept, and you may just have let some in. The Cutter comes in on the Regatta Course, still racing, and you have to stop her. When she finally slows, Dunnage fires the gun. Every sail fills at once. The little Plucky Prue, which jumped the start thirty years ago, finishes its race at last. Dunnage rewards you with a rosette, bowls of chowder and 1800 Marks, and a small red-and-gold pennant on the lighthouse mast reads "Next stop, Saltglass. Midsummer Fair, at noon." The Noon Gnomon, still telling noon What happens East of Brindle Quay the road turns to white salt, and Saltglass Fair stands in a noon that has not moved in thirty years. Not one shadow shifts. Mayoress Noon welcomes you warmly: Hesper Quill's poster promised that the best of the day need never end, the town took a vote, and even the sundials voted yes. Each Dial-Keeper holds a pole up to the light so no shadow can slip. At the top of the Glass Hill, the Noon Gnomon, built by the Company of Clockmakers a hundred years ago, has told twelve o'clock ever since. Its observatory door is sun-locked, and only the Company's Dial Key opens it. Three of the Company are at the Fair: Master Orme, Dunstan Rook and Imelda Frayne. This is Corwin's chapter. Corwin told his friends at Hollowmere that the Company put him out of its ranks nine years ago. He walked out. In the pavilion the full story comes out. Master Orme says he told Corwin to go home as a kindness, and Corwin heard it as a sentence. The Company did nothing when Master Venn built his idea of a clock to stop every clock, and from outside, nothing looked exactly like taking his side. Corwin admits that he took his fear to the Council so someone bigger could say no, and called that courage. Nobody came after him; he never looked back to see. Ottoline gets her own answer: Professor Lisle wrote to the Company for eleven years, and Orme read every letter and had no reply that was not "we were wrong." Orme gives Corwin the Dial Key, saying that the Rules allow it to go to any hand a Master would trust with his own bench. His bench by the window has been kept dusted. Dunstan gives him back his old brass loupe. Corwin says he is not coming back to the Company yet, and Orme says the bench stays. Up the Glass Hill, the Dial Key opens the observatory. The Gnomon is at the bottom, and a bronze shutter blocks the corridor until the sun speaks. In the east wing, the Hall of Mirrors has three levers and a sign: the sun sees itself in three. Two mirrors lean forward to listen, and one stands back to look. When the beam strikes the dial, the shutter rises. The Noon Gnomon is holding the hour and has forgotten how to let go. You fight, and when it falls its pole tilts a hair off true and a long thin shadow slides across the great dial for the first time in thirty years. Down at the Fair, every shadow stirs and stretches away east. The Dial-Keepers lower their poles, Cecily Brine sets off for the forty paces to her sister's tea stall, and Mayoress Noon finds that her shadow has a hat. Orme thanks Corwin, and Corwin promises to try Thursday. Party and moth Nobody joins or leaves this chapter. Bonds rise most between Wren and Corwin, and Corwin with Bett and Ottoline. What happens You step out of the Fair's east gate into the Lantern Fields, and the first thing Bett notices is that the music smells like a wedding. Master Snuff, the Master of Ceremonies, greets the party in the square with great warmth and no sense of time. The bride left her house at dusk, the groom went out to meet her, and everyone has been waiting for them to reach the chapel ever since. It is still dusk, thirty years later. Snuff explains that the Wedding Bells, a peal of bell-machines in the chapel belfry, ring the bride in: one toll for every step. Nobody has told them what to do when she arrives. Sabine Averill, a retired lamplighter and guest of the family, explains the rest. Not one lamp in town has gone out since the wedding day, and a day cannot end while all its lamps are lit. She would like to put out the three lamps on the chapel porch, which hold the door latched, but the road is thick with Rust and her snuffer-pole is not a weapon. She joins you. Dame Maud Taper, the bride's mother, has been holding her daughter's bouquet for thirty years. The roses have gone gold at the edges and never wilted. You carry them east along the Chapel Road to Marigold Taper, who walks with her groom Alder Wick one very small step to each toll. If she steps early, the road grows longer. The last time she counted four hundred and twelve steps, it turned out to be four hundred and thirteen. Marigold admits what she fears most: arriving, and finding that the next day is only an ordinary Tuesday. Alder says he would very much like that Tuesday, and a sandwich on a bench. She asks you to stop the Bells, not break them. At the end of the road Sabine snuffs the three porch lamps, in any order, and the chapel door unlatches. Inside, three bell-ropes on the walls (north-west, north-east and a small one in the east vestry) wake the clockwork and lift the brass gate across the chancel steps. Behind the gate the ceiling is hundreds of bells hung in a swinging lattice around a round brass dial. Ottoline sees what is wrong: the Rust has gathered round the one note it cannot make, like dust round a stopped clock. Wren asks it nicely, and you fight. When the Bells fall quiet, the lattice swings in one wide arc and every bell rings at once, and then once more, softly, to the last bell on the left. That is the last peal the machine was missing. You step onto the porch into a different evening, deep blue and full of stars. Marigold comes up the road at a happy, slightly too-fast step with her mother's roses in her fist, shouting that she counted four hundred and twelve (Alder says thirteen). The wedding finally happens, the Bells ring one clear note for the last step, and Sabine goes down the road snuffing lamps while the town lights up window by window. There is a first dance on the cobbles. Even Corwin, who insists he does not dance,

s: Quick answers about fights, saving, difficulty and side activities, plus a short list of tips for each stage of the game.
x: Home The Roads Between Reference FAQ and tips FAQ and tips Quick answers about fights, saving, difficulty and side activities, plus a short list of tips for each stage of the game. Updated 11 November 2026 Note The Roads Between is in closed testing. Answers describe the game as it stands today and may change. Questions How long is the game? About thirty to forty hours if you do everything, with the main story a good part of that. Chapters 1 to 14 are playable today. Are there random battles? No. You see the Rust on the map and choose whether to touch it. I lost a fight. Do I lose progress? No. You can try the battle again or go back to your last save. The Settings page has a Story difficulty if you would rather breeze through. See Training and difficulty . Why is the boss so hard? Bosses are tuned to need a few extra fights. It is normal to lose the first attempt. A few extra levels turn it into a fair fight. Where can I save? At a bed, a camp or a save clock (a small clock face set in a wall). The game also saves automatically whenever you go through a door. Why did the Rust come back? Most Rust returns after you rest. Rust standing near a save clock or camp stays beaten, and one-off guards, elites and bosses never return. I cannot find a chest. It may be a hidden chest, shown only once the moth has learned Seek (Chapter 2) and you walk close. What does the moth do in battle? It never attacks. Its Lights show big moves coming, show weaknesses, let a friend go sooner, shake off a Seized hero once, and in the end heal everyone once a fight. See The lantern moth and its Lights . Is there a card game? Yes: Cogs , taught in Chapter 14. Can I cook? You can learn recipes and receive meals from Chapter 11. The cooking pot at camps is not open yet. See Cooking . Can I fish? Yes, from Chapter 12. See Fishing . Do I need to play the other BlairsLab games? No. The world is shared, and a few places are glimpsed in the others, but nothing in this game depends on them. Which way up is the game? Landscape. The controls are on Controls and menus . Does this site spoil the story? Only on pages marked with spoilers. Each chapter has a region guide with none and a separate plot and boss page with all of it. Tips by stage Early on 1. Talk to everyone. Many people say where to go next. 2. Fight the small Rust first and keep a few Tonics and Oil Cans in the bag. 3. Rest at the save clock before every boss. Through Part One 1. Check the Almanac and Moth pages in the menu whenever something new happens. 2. Use Seek's weakness display, and bring a mix of Spark, Frost and Tide. 3. Spend Mainspring points as you level: unspent points do nothing. 4. Check each new shop before you spend your Marks elsewhere. See Shops . 5. Visit the smith and make Cogs from your Rust Scrap. See Growth and crafting . From Chapter 11 1. Take the optional elite and hunt of each region once you are comfortably above the level of the area. 2. Keep your cooking ingredients: buff meals are strong before a boss. 3. Cogs and the Arena are optional, but both pay well and both can be left until you are ready. In any fight 1. Guard before a BIG move. 2. Fill Chimes: act often and let your front line take hits. 3. Bett's Drop Anchor plus a Guard keeps the whole party out of trouble. 4. Do not flee from a boss: you cannot. Heal and try again. Previous Glossary

s: Every BlairsLab game is set in the Evenwold. This is how the games fit together and the rules we follow when we link them.
x: Every BlairsLab game is set in the same country, the Evenwold . It has towns on branch lines, hop fields, a wharf, a flooded valley, a moor and a city that has been stopped at one second to midnight. Some games send you travelling across it, and others stay inside a single tower, belfry or workshop. In all of them time is a material, and craftspeople can wind it, hold it and rewind it. You don't need to know any of this to play. It's here if you're curious. The rules we keep We set ourselves a few rules so that the shared world never becomes homework. Every game is complete on its own. You never need another game's story to follow the one you're playing. Links between games are small. You might see a city in the distance, find a letter or notice a creature passing through. One game's story never causes or explains another's. Owning more than one game gets you nothing extra. There are no cross-save bonuses, codes, shared currencies or locked doors. People and memories are never currency or loot in any game. You are never punished for missing a day. The lantern moth is in every game , and it looks the same in all of them. The stories are about tradespeople and neighbours. There is no chosen hero and no gore. Where to go next The games introduces each game and says where it is set. The world covers the places and how time works. Recurring things covers moths, clocks, lamps and the Rust. Where games touch lists the links between games. It has spoilers. Or go straight to a game: Hivewright , The Last Bell , The Last Second Workshop , The Lamplighter , The Belfry Gun or The Roads Between .

s: The Evenwold is the country every BlairsLab game is set in. This page covers its places and how time works there.
x: Home The Evenwold The world The world The Evenwold is the country every BlairsLab game is set in. This page covers its places and how time works there. On this page Time is a material Places that have stopped Places you can visit Clocks keep places going How the games look The games are set in a country called the Evenwold . It has old roads, hop fields, a wharf, a flooded valley, a moor, a city stopped in time and a hill town at that city's wall. The "even" in the name comes from evenfall, the hour when the lamps are lit and the moths come out, and from keeping time even. Nobody in the Evenwold counts years, and none of the games gives a date. Time is a material In the Evenwold, time can be worked like brass or glass. Clockmakers wind it and keepers hold it. A good workshop can fold it, and a good bell can ring it backwards. The people who do this are tradespeople , such as couriers, keepers, gunners, lamplighters and clockmakers. There are no wizards. Places that have stopped A lot of the Evenwold has stopped. There was no single disaster, and the places stopped for different reasons. Some places are held . Someone stopped them on purpose and stays to tend them. Some places ran down . One morning nobody came to wind the clock, and nobody has since. The Rust gathers where time has been left alone. The games don't explain it further. Places you can visit Place Game What it is Meridia The Last Second Workshop A city held at 23:59:59. The rain has stopped in mid-air and the last train is stuck between stations. The great clock tower Hivewright A tower tall enough that its top is in cloud. Its clocks stopped one dawn, and a hive of wind-ups is climbing it and restarting them. The valley of stopped clocks The Last Bell A valley where every clock stopped on the same evening, except the bell in one small stone tower. Belcourt The Belfry Gun A hill town under a belfry, just outside the edge of Meridia's held second. The road to the wall The Lamplighter A long road towards the city wall that you light one lamp at a time. The back roads The Roads Between Small towns on old railway lines, in the country between the great clocks. Clocks keep places going A place in the Evenwold depends on its clocks and bells. Great clocks restart the floors of a tower, bells call the hour, and Meridia's station clock must never move. When a clock stops, the place around it is affected. How the games look The Last Second Workshop is drawn in navy and brass, Hivewright in amber and verdigris, and The Last Bell in dusk blue and bronze. Lamps, clock faces, letters and small brass mechanisms appear in all of them. Previous The games Next Recurring things

s: The lantern moth, wind-ups, the Rust, clocks and lamps all appear in more than one BlairsLab game.
x: Home The Evenwold Recurring things Recurring things The lantern moth, wind-ups, the Rust, clocks and lamps all appear in more than one BlairsLab game. On this page The lantern moth Light that leaks between seconds Clocks, bells and lamps Wind-ups The Rust Resets with a reason A few things appear in more than one game. The lantern moth The lantern moth is the only creature that is in every BlairsLab game. It is small, made of soft light, and drawn to places where time is under strain. It acts as a guide and a companion. The same rules apply to it in every game. It is never a weapon, it is never sold or fed, and nothing happens to it while you are away. Owning another game doesn't make it stronger. Its job is different in each game. Game What the moth does The Last Second Workshop Appears when your taps land perfectly, and walks the map to guide you Hivewright Flies to the busiest part of the hive and lights it up, glowing brighter at every great clock The Last Bell Settles on one of your towers to make it truer, and is the one thing that stays put when the bell rewinds The Belfry Gun Once a run, settles on the wall and mends it when it is nearly gone The Lamplighter Once a night, flares to save you The games still in testing have a moth too. Light that leaks between seconds Two of the games say that the moths come from light that leaks between one second and the next. No game says more about their origin than that. Clocks, bells and lamps Great clocks, small bells, station clocks and lamps are in every game, and they are what keeps a place running. There are four bells across the games, and they are four different bells. Wind-ups Wind-ups are small clockwork creatures. Many different craftspeople made them, and nobody agrees on how they came to be a little bit alive. Some are friendly. In some games the Rust has got into the springs of others and made them hostile. Those ones are broken, and in some games you can mend them. The Rust The Rust is a rusty clockwork growth that coats things and wakes old machines as broken, restless wind-ups. It is in most of the games and none of them explains it. We have left it unexplained on purpose. Resets with a reason Every game has a reset, and the story gives a reason for each one. The workshop Folds, the hive Rewinds, and the bell rings backwards. A reset rearranges things, but the people keep their worth and you keep what you have learned. s: The places where one BlairsLab game shows you something from another, such as a distant city, a far light or a familiar face.
x: Home The Evenwold Where games touch Where games touch The places where one BlairsLab game shows you something from another, such as a distant city, a far light or a familiar face. Spoilers ahead. This page discusses story events and reveals. Come back after you have played if you want to find things out yourself. On this page A city seen from far away Lights and letters Faces that turn up twice Towers that look alike What we do not do These are the places where one game shows you something from another. They are always seen from a distance, and you don't need any of them to follow a game. Note This page mentions late-game moments from several games. If you would rather find these yourself, come back after you have played. A city seen from far away The held city of Meridia can be seen from several other games. In The Last Bell , one of the last story pages looks out from the high window to a tall tower with a lamp at its top, and beyond it a city standing still in the rain. In Hivewright , the first great clock sends a thought out past a city wall where rain hangs in the air, to someone who may be looking up at a new light. In The Belfry Gun , Belcourt's belfry stands on its hill just outside the city's edge, below Meridia's frozen skyline. Lights and letters The Last Second Workshop has "eighteen lights beyond the wall", a single light turning slowly on a coast that is on no map, and a final line that says another clock answers yours. Hivewright has the other side of this. In its later floors the hive sees far lights and a lighthouse sweeping the edge of a sea, and blinks its own lamp back. A sealed letter found in the tower is addressed to "the keeper beyond the wall" and is never opened. No game says what the eighteen lights are. Faces that turn up twice In The Belfry Gun , some people from the Workshop's city have come out to help hold Belcourt's wall. They are Iona, Mara Vale, the Keeper, Senn the courier and Edda Rook the lighthouse keeper. They are the same people as in the Workshop, but you don't need to have played it. Towers that look alike The tall, lit towers are different towers. The one at the top of the great clock tower in Hivewright and the lamp on the road in The Lamplighter are different places, seen from different parts of the country. The tower with a lamp that the keeper of The Last Bell sees far across the hills is never named. What we do not do These links are never requirements. No game unlocks anything in another, and no game explains another's mysteries. To the people in each story, the other games are only distant lights. Previous Recurring things

s: Why this site may show ads, what that means for you, and how to choose.
x: At the moment this site shows no ads and sets no advertising cookies. Why ads? BlairsLab is a very small studio. Our games are free to start, and this site, with its guides, characters and lore, takes real time to write and keep up to date. Ads on the site help pay for that, and for the next game. Our promises Ads never gate content. You never need to watch, click or close anything to read a page. Ads are clearly labelled and kept away from the first thing you read, so they do not jump the layout around. You have a choice about ad cookies and personalised ads. See below. Ads on the site do not change the games. Nothing in a game is hidden behind this site. Cookies and personalised ads If ads are switched on, they come from Google AdSense, whose partners may use cookies. In the EEA, the UK and Switzerland we will ask you before setting any. Full details, and how to opt out of personalised ads, are on the privacy and cookies page . Problem ads If you see an ad that is offensive, misleading or broken, please tell us with the page it was on. We can block advertisers and ad types. Ad blockers You are free to use one. The site works the same either way. If you like what we do and would rather support us another way, buying one of our games or telling a friend helps just as much.

s: What this website does and does not collect, how ads and cookies work if they are switched on, and how to reach us.
x: This page covers the website at blairslabgames.co.nz. Our mobile games have their own privacy policies (linked from the game's store page and, where available, from the footer of this site), and those are the ones that apply when you play. At the moment this site shows no ads and sets no advertising cookies. What we collect on this site No accounts, no sign-up, no forms. You can read everything without telling us who you are. Visitor counts. We use Cloudflare Web Analytics to count page views, so we can see which pages are read. It sets no cookies, does not fingerprint you and does not follow you across sites. It records the page address, the site that linked you here, and general details such as country, browser type and how fast the page loaded. Your theme choice. If you press the light/dark toggle, your browser stores that choice (in "local storage") so the next page matches. It never leaves your device and we cannot see it. Server logs. The site is a plain set of static files served by our hosting provider. Like any web host, the provider may keep ordinary technical logs, such as your IP address, the page requested and the time, for security and operation. We do not use these logs to identify or follow individual visitors. Search. The search box runs entirely in your browser. What you type is not sent anywhere.
